title: Elliot Graham Dies: Oscar-Nominated ‘Milk’ Editor Was 50
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Rose Friedman Dies: NPR Arts Editor & ‘Books We Love’ Co-Creator Was 38 Cate Blanchett Asks London Audience To Stop Filming Play, Says Stage Is Place “Where We Can Simply Be Together And Be Present” Editors Guild Praises California’s New Post-Production Tax Credit Law As “Historic” View All September 22, 2026 6:53am Elliot Graham (2022) Joe Maher/Getty Images Elliot Graham, the Oscar-nominated film editor for Milk whose credits also included Steve Jobs, No Time To Die, Superman Returns and Captain Marvel , died Saturday, September 19, in Los Angeles. He was 50. Graham died by suicide, according to the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner . Born in Claremont, California, on June 8, 1976, Graham launched his show business career in the early 2000s with the feature film The Last Minute (2001) and the TV series House (2004). He moved into big-budget feature projects with 2006’s Superman Returns . Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries News Rose Friedman Dies: NPR Arts Editor & ‘Books We Love’ Co-Creator Was 38 Two years later he was hired by edit Milk , the Harvey Milk bio-pic written by Dustin Lance Black and directed by Gus Van Sant. Starring Sean Penn, Milk was nominated for eight Oscars, including for Graham’s editing. (Black and Penn won their categories). Watch on Deadline “The movie Milk wouldn’t have come together in the way it did without the amazing work of our editor Elliot Graham,” Milk producer Dan Jinks wrote in a tribute on Facebook . “He was nominated for an Oscar for his role.” “I have so many thoughts and feelings about this sweet, kind and quirky man,” Jinks continued. “For now, I’ll just say rest in peace Elliot.” After Milk , Graham worked again with Van Sant on the 2011 film Restless starring Mia Wasikowska. He also edited an episode of the Kelsey Grammer series Boss that year. Additional credits include Steve Jobs (2015), Molly’s Game starring Jessica Chastain (2017), Captain Marvel (2019) and No Time To Die , the 2021 James Bond film starring Daniel Craig. Graham and editor Tom Cross shared a BAFTA award for their work on the film. In addition to his editing credit for the 2018 FX limited series Trust , the Danny Boyle-directed project about the kidnapping of John Paul Getty III, Graham also served as producer. Graham also provided additional editing on X2: X-Men United (2003) and The Amazing Spider-Man 2 (2014). title: Former Cinecittà Chief Nicola Maccanico Appointed CEO of Rainbow Group’s Colorado Film
full_text: Sep 22, 2026 6:52am PT Former Cinecittà Chief Nicola Maccanico Appointed CEO of Rainbow Group’s Colorado Film By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Oscars: Egypt Selects Abu Bakr Shawky’s ‘The Stories’ for International Feature Race 5 hours ago Red Sea Film Festival Cancels 2026 Edition, Will Return Next Year 1 day ago Dubai Film Festival Revived With New Edition Set for December 2027 5 days ago See All Courtesy Colorado Films Former Cinecittà Studios chief Nicola Maccanico has been appointed CEO of Rome-based production shingle Colorado Film. The company is owned and operated by Italy’s Rainbow Group, led by Iginio Straffi , creator of the hit “Winx Club” animation franchise. Maccanico, who is a former Warner Bros. and Sky Italia senior exec, spearheaded the radical overhaul of Cinecittà’s Rome studios for three years. He stepped down in 2024 after Italy’s right-wing government decided to change the studios’ management team. Related Stories Billy Bush to Join Fox News as Contributor Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago Colorado Film is a commercially successful live-action movies shingle that in 2024 scored a hit with young adult romantic drama “The Tearsmith,” which became the first Netflix Italy original to reach the No. 1 slot on the streamer’s global movie chart in the non-English-language category. Besides “The Tearsmith,” Colorado’s top titles over the years comprise the smash-hit “Me Contro Te” comedy franchise, featuring two Sicilian YouTube sensations; blockbuster comedy “La Peggior Settimana della Mia Vita”; theatrical saga “Ten Days Without Mom”; and bestselling Italian mystery writer Donato Carrisi’s directorial debut “The Girl in the Fog.” Popular on Variety Colorado’s upcoming productions include English-language rom-com “Blame It on Rome,” directed by Francesco Carrozzini and starring Michele Morrone (“365 Days”) and Gabrielle Union (“Bad Boys II”). It’s co-produced by Colorado Film, Nebraska and Amazon MGM Studios as an original for Prime Video Italy. Maccanico will replace Colorado’s outgoing CEO Thomas J. Ciampa, who has just been appointed chief of Vision Distribution, the Italian theatrical distributor jointly operated by Sky Italia and five prominent Italian production companies. “Nicola Maccanico’s appointment is part of Rainbow Group’s ongoing growth strategy and is aimed at further strengthening Colorado Film’s position within the Italian and international audiovisual industry, building on its creative heritage and developing new production opportunities,” Rainbow Group said in a statement. “Nicola Maccanico’s arrival marks the driving force behind a new strategic phase for the future of Colorado Film,” said Straffi, Rainbow Group’s president. “His extensive expertise and ability to combine creative vision with industrial strategy will be crucial to the company’s expansion.” Straffi added, “We will continue to invest in talent and in Italian creative excellence, driven by the ambition to ensure these stories resonate powerfully with audiences both in Italy and internationally.” Commented Maccanico: “Contributing to the development of Colorado Film is an important challenge, and having the opportunity to do so alongside an entrepreneur with the visionary talent of Iginio Straffi is a privilege. The audiovisual market needs Italian production companies with an industrial mindset, capable of growing and becoming increasingly competitive. The festival previously launched in Latin America in 2024 and expanded across Asia in 2025. This year’s lineup includes six presentations: two live broadcasts of the BTS World Tour “Arirang,” concert films from Seventeen , Tomorrow X Together and Enhypen, and the interactive “HYBE Cheering Party” in 3D. Related Stories Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago Maria Bartiromo Out at Fox News, Fox Business The BTS broadcasts will stream from Buenos Aires, marking the group’s first performance in Argentina, on Oct. 24 in the Americas and Oct. 25 in the rest of the world. A second BTS broadcast from São Paulo, the finale of the group’s Latin American tour, will screen Oct. 30 in the Americas and Oct. 31 elsewhere. Popular on Variety Seventeen’s film captures the group’s “New” world tour, while Tomorrow X Together’s entry documents “Act : Tomorrow,” its fourth global tour. Enhypen’s film revisits the Seoul concert that opened the “Blood Saga” tour. The “HYBE Cheering Party” screening lets audiences sing along to on-screen lyrics and wave light sticks to music videos from artists including BTS, Seventeen, Tomorrow X Together, Enhypen, Le Sserafim, &Team, Boynextdoor, TWS, Illit, Katseye, aoen, Cortis and Santos Bravos. Tickets go on sale Sept. 30. “Following the incredible response to HYBE Cine Fest across Latin America and Asia, we are scaling this festival format to global cinema audiences,” said Marc Allenby, chief executive officer of Trafalgar Releasing. “Bringing together major concert films, interactive 3D cheering parties, and landmark live broadcasts across a single week gives fans everywhere an unprecedented way to celebrate their favorite HYBE artists together in cinemas.” The festival’s Special Location program, which offers interactive fan zones, merchandise and pop-up stores at select cinemas, is expanding into North America and Europe this year after previously running in Latin America and Asia. Trafalgar Releasing operates in more than 15,000 cinemas across 132 countries and has distributed concert films for artists including Taylor Swift, Beyoncé and Metallica. HYBE’s roster spans labels including Bighit Music, Belift Lab, Source Music and Pledis Entertainment. title: ‘The Future of Spanish Cinema Is Not About Making More Films’: Atresmedia Unveils Broad Slate
full_text: Sep 22, 2026 6:45am PT ‘The Future of Spanish Cinema Is Not About Making More Films’: Atresmedia Unveils Broad Slate From 'La Bola Negra' to 'La Roja,' Atresmedia Makes Its Case for Bigger, Bolder Spanish Cinema By Callum McLennan Plus Icon Callum McLennan Latest Inside the Basque Production Boom: Who Owns the Growth? 8 hours ago ‘The Harvester’ Star Antonio de la Torre: ‘Violence Has No Justification, but It Does Have an Explanation’ 9 hours ago San Sebastian Startup Challenge Puts AI, Immersive Tech and Green Production in Focus 9 hours ago See All 'La Bola Negra' Carla Oset/Netflix SAN SEBASTIAN, Spain — Spanish theatrical audiences are concentrating around fewer films, with nearly 75% of admissions this year going to just 10 local titles despite more than 275 Spanish films being released, according to Atresmedia Cine general manager Jaime Ortiz de Artiñano. “Audiences have become far more selective,” Ortiz de Artiñano told Variety ahead of Atresmedia’s San Sebastián presentation. “They are willing to leave home for films that feel like true cultural events.” Related Stories Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago Billy Bush to Join Fox News as Contributor Atresmedia Cine, which Ortiz de Artiñano says has led the Spanish box office for the past seven years with market shares ranging from around 30% to more than 50%, sees that concentration as reshaping what theatrical success requires. Popular on Variety “For me, this leads to a very clear conclusion: the future of Spanish cinema is not about making more films, but about making films that more people want to see,” he said. That thinking was on display at the Hotel Maria Cristina’s Salon Elcano in San Sebastián, where Atresmedia presented a slate spanning the return of Adriana Ugarte in “Sira,” thriller “Trazos ocultos” and Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s “ La Bola Negra ,” where it has partnered on the film, taking free-to-air TV rights. The event was Atresmedia Cine’s traditional annual industry presentation during the festival, moderated by journalist David Martos, with a host of actors among them Goya winners Eduard Fernández, and Javier Gutiérrez, both in good sprits, and filmmakers Roberto Bueso, Aritz Moreno, Álvaro Fernández Armero and Daniel Calparsoro with their projects. “Sira” brings Adriana Ugarte (“Julieta”) back with sequel to “The Time In Between Seams” as Sira Quiroga, moving the period drama into the aftermath of World War II and across Jerusalem, London, Madrid and Tangier. Produced by Buendía Estudios Bizkaia with the participation of Atresmedia and Netflix, it will premiere first on Atresplayer before moving to Antena 3 primetime, an increasingly important windowing model for the broadcaster. “Trazos ocultos,” starring Toni Acosta and Rodolfo Sancho, forms the other major series play presented at the festival, underscoring Atresmedia’s continuing bet on broad appeal premium fiction that can travel between subscription and linear television. On the film side, Spain’s Oscar submission “La Bola Negra” and TIFF People’s Choice Award winner, points to a more international model. The Lorca-inspired drama, directed by Calvo and Ambrossi and starring Guitarricadelafuente, Penélope Cruz, Miguel Bernardeau, Lola Dueñas and Glenn Close, is a Movistar Plus original produced with Suma Content Films, El Deseo and Le Pacte, with the participation of Atresmedia. For Ortiz de Artiñano, the film’s festival trajectory has gone beyond initial expectations. “In more than twenty-five years working in this industry, I have rarely seen a project gather this level of momentum,” he said, pointing to Cannes, Toronto and San Sebastián. That international reach sits alongside a more hard-headed reading of the Spanish theatrical market. Atresmedia says its films account for more than 50% of Spanish-film box office in 2026, with “Torrente Presidente” alone representing almost 40%. That logic also shapes financing. Ortiz de Artiñano argues that broadcasters, platforms, distributors and independent producers increasingly need to combine forces around ambitious projects. “No single player can consistently finance ambitious films on its own anymore,” he said. Atresmedia’s expanding 2027 slate, from “La Roja” and “El Confidente” to “Caza Mayor,” suggests the company sees its role increasingly as both producer and industrial catalyst: assembling partners, reducing risk and helping Spanish projects reach the scale needed to compete for attention at home and abroad. Below we profile the upcoming projects: “La Bola Negra” dir. Javier Calvo, Javier Ambrossi (Movistar Plus+, Suma Content Films, El Deseo, Le Pacte) Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi direct a multi-generational drama tracing the interconnected lives of three men across three different periods. Guitarricadelafuente, Miguel Bernardeau and Carlos González lead a cast that also includes Penélope Cruz, Lola Dueñas and Glenn Close. Written by Calvo, Ambrossi and Alberto Conejero, the film explores sexuality, desire, pain and inheritance through a three-part story linked to one of Federico García Lorca’s final unfinished works as well as the subject of his near last love poems. “ The Blind Ants “ ( “Las Ciegas Hormigas,” “Inurri Itsuak”) dir. Igor Legarreta (Lamia Producciones, Lamia Films, Lapona Zinema, Lazona Producciones, Bruja del Norte AIE, Buendía Estudios Bizkaia, Sideral Cinema, Caviar Antwerp B.V.) Igor Legarreta directs and co-writes this 1935-set Basque drama starring Urko Olazábal, Itziar Ituño, Josean Bengoetxea, Miren Gaztañaga and Carlos Santos. When a violent storm grounds an English ship carrying tons of coal off Algorta, Sabas Jauregui sees a chance to save his family from winter and drags his children into the dangerous salvage effort despite his wife Josefa’s fears. The struggle to protect the recovered “black gold” becomes a test of survival, desperation and family loyalty. “Karateka” dir. Aritz Moreno (Atresmedia Cine, Sr.&Sra., Karateka A.I.E., Wrong Men, Apaches Entertainment, Colosé Producciones) Aritz Moreno (“Advantages of Travelling by Train”) directs an inspirational sports drama chronicling Sandra Sánchez’s journey from Talavera de la Reina to Olympic gold in Tokyo at 39. Andrea Ros stars opposite Patrick Criado as Sánchez’s coach and partner Jesús del Moral. Shot across Spain and Japan, the film combines elite competition, romance and resilience in the true story of one of karate’s defining champions. “ El mal padre ” dir. Roberto Bueso (MOD Producciones, MOD Pictures, Misent Producciones, Atresmedia Cine) Eduard Fernández leads Roberto Bueso’s family drama as a celebrated writer who gathers his estranged children before Christmas at the coastal holiday home where they spent their childhood summers. Adam Jezierski, Francesco Carril, Meritxell Calvo and Cristina Plazas co-star. Selected for San Sebastián’s Official Selection, the film explores abandonment, resentment and impending parenthood as one fractured family is forced to confront the past. “The Confidant” (“El confidente”) dir. Daniel Calparsoro (Bowfinger International Pictures, Esto También Pasará, El Confidente Films AIE, Lionceau Films) Daniel Calparsoro directs a fact-inspired thriller starring Javier Gutiérrez and Miguel Herrán as a veteran policeman and his young informant, two men divided by principle but bound by loyalty and loneliness. Scripted by Fernando Navarro, the Spain-France production unfolds against a dangerous police operation and will world premiere in Seminci’s Official Selection, screening out of competition. “La Roja” dir. Marcel Barrena (Atresmedia Cine, Beta Fiction Spain, Vilaüt Films, La Roja AIE) Marcel Barrena directs and co-writes this fact-inspired underdog sports drama starring Paco León as a coach attempting to turn Spain into a competitive cricket nation. Carolina Yuste co-stars alongside Atul Vijayakumar and an ensemble including several debutants. Shot in Barcelona, the film uses cricket to explore integration, cultural difference, belonging and an evolving idea of what representing Spain can mean. “Big Game Hunt” (“Caza mayor”) dir. Daniel Sánchez Arévalo (Movistar Plus+, La Película del Tigre A.I.E., Estela Films, Tenampa Films, Cut One, Pólvora Films, Tinnitus) Daniel Sánchez Arévalo directs a rural thriller with black-comedy overtones starring Antonio de la Torre. He plays an Extremaduran pig herder who returns home covered in blood claiming to have seen a tiger, setting off an increasingly strange reckoning in Fregenal de la Sierra. Written by María Ballesteros and José Antonio de Pascual, the film turns an impossible sighting into a test of truth and desperation. “Caer de Pie” dir. Salvador Calvo (Atresmedia Cine, Fonte Films, LAZONA, Cómo Volé AIE) Salvador Calvo directs a fact-based drama starring Marina Salas as Ana, a 30-year-old woman admitted to psychiatric care after reaching breaking point and attempting suicide. Written by Alejandro Hernández, the film follows her 37-day hospitalization and gradual confrontation with vulnerability and recovery. Daniel Ibañez, Carmen Ruiz, Pedro Casablanc and Alicia Borrachero feature in the ensemble. “The Professor” (“El profesor”) dir. Daniel Castro (Atresmedia Cine, Gonita, 4 Cats Pictures, Una Nueva Comedia AIE, Vaya Films) Javier Gutiérrez headlines Daniel Castro’s Spain-Colombia production as a lonely university professor who falls for a Colombian model 20 years his junior despite her refusal to appear on video. Written and directed by Castro, the digital-age relationship story is in post-production, with Film Factory Entertainment handling international sales and A Contracorriente Films distributing in Spain. “Todo por la Casa” dir. María Togores (Atresmedia Cine, Beta Fiction Spain, Chef Sin Desperdicio 2022 AIE) Spain’s housing squeeze fuels María Togores’ romantic comedy starring Silvia Alonso and Alejandro García as desperate Madrid renters who pose as a conventional couple to secure an apartment from traditional-minded landlords. Written by Olatz Arroyo, the film turns an acute contemporary housing problem into the engine for a high-concept relationship comedy, with the deception complicated by the landlords living directly opposite. “Matar a Ramón” dir. Álvaro Fernández Armero (Atresmedia Cine, Un Pueblo Tranquilo AIE, La Terraza Films, True Crime Factory, Ikiru Films) Álvaro Fernández Armero directs a rural mystery-comedy about Ramón, a La Mancha contractor who survives a bizarre hit-and-run only to suffer a string of increasingly suspicious accidents. The ensemble includes Óscar de la Fuente, Carla Díaz, Yaël Belicha, Israel Elejalde and José Mota. Written by Daniel Castro and Diego Soto, the film pairs an attention-seeking Guardia Civil veteran with a socially awkward rookie investigating what may be their first “serial victim.” “Entre olas” dir. Chloé Wallace (Atresmedia Cine, Buendía Estudios Canarias, La Pepa Films, Basque Films, Xoelius and Veguchini, Ocean Love Story AIE) Chloé Wallace directs a romantic coming-of-age story starring Carla Tous, Nuno Gallego and Jan Buxaderas. Shot in Tenerife, the film centers on a summer love triangle in which surfing and environmental awareness become increasingly central. As an ecological threat emerges, Ali’s choice between stability and freedom expands into a larger reckoning with identity, belonging and the island’s future. “A morte nos teus ollos” dir. Guillermo de Oliveira (Atresmedia Cine, Sideral, Sétima) Guillermo de Oliveira makes his fiction feature debut with a fact-inspired Galician thriller starring Pepe Lorente and Iván Marcos. Developed through the Spanish Film Academy’s Residencies program and shot around Vigo and Pontevedra, the 1990s-set story follows two compromised policemen whose robbery scheme spirals into a tale of corruption, family, violence, greed, guilt and power. “La Dona Invisible” dir. Cristina Fernández Pintado (Atresmedia Cine, The Fly Hunter, La Terraza Films, Sucedió en Valverde AIE) Cristina Fernández Pintado directs a comic mystery starring Mona Martínez as Mihaela, a Romanian cleaner nearing retirement who discovers a dead civil servant in the government offices where she works. When police dismiss the death as accidental, the crime-fiction obsessive launches her own investigation alongside an eccentric young intern, probing both a possible murder and the opaque, rule-bound world of public bureaucracy. title: Oscar Best Picture Category Will Soon Be Dominated by International Films, Claims ‘I’m Still Here’ Producer Rodrigo Teixeira
full_text: Sep 22, 2026 6:31am PT Oscar Best Picture Category Will Soon Be Dominated by International Films, Claims ‘I’m Still Here’ Producer Rodrigo Teixeira The RT Films boss was speaking at the Creative Investors' Conference in San Sebastian By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Will Record Summer Box Office Save Indie Cinema? Not Quite, but Cannes Might, Say U.S. Producers 3 hours ago U.K.’s National Film and TV School and Sean Connery Foundation to Establish Permanent Base in Edinburgh (EXCLUSIVE) 5 hours ago Netflix Partners With British Library, Sets Talks Series With Florence Pugh, Zoe Kazan and More 15 hours ago See All Credit: Alile Dara Onawale - Globoplay U.S. films will soon be the minority among the nominees for the top Academy Award, claims one of South America’s most successful producers. Rodrigo Teixeira , who through his RT Films banner has produced the likes of “Frances Ha,” “Call Me by Your Name,” “Ad Astra” “Bergman Island” and “I’m Still Here,” building up long-standing relationships with filmmakers such as James Gray in the process, made the claim at the San Sebastian Film Festival ‘s Creative Investors’ Conference, co-organized by CAA Media Finance. Related Stories Maria Bartiromo Out at Fox News, Fox Business Billy Bush to Join Fox News as Contributor “We are [now] seeing at least three-four international films in the best film category,” he said, speaking on Tuesday. “And in five years from now, I believe international films will make up 60% of the category for best film. I truly believe that. Because we can talk more. We have freedom of speech, and in the U.S., without freedom of speech, it’s difficult to get financed. But outside the U.S. we have it, and I believe in five years the international films are going to be bigger than American films.” Popular on Variety Teixeira is an Oscar nominee himself, having produced Walter Salles’ Brazillan smash hit “I’m Still Here,” which in 2025 was nominated for best picture and best actress (for Fernanda Torres) and won the Oscar for best international feature. The film would also earn more than $36 million (from a budget of around $9 million), becoming the highest-grossing Brazilian film since COVID. “I’m Still Here,” claimed Teixeira, was part of a wave of cinema from Brazil made in the wake of the “very hardcore, right-wing” Bolsonaro government and served as as “an act of hope” that helped “change the self-esteem of the country.” Teixeira was recently in Cannes with his latest Gray collaboration and competition title “Paper Tiger,” which he said he originated, and Director’s Fortnight entry “La Perra” from Dominga Sotomayor, which would win the Palm Dog Award. Coming up for RT is Gray’s next project and Mia Hansen-Love’s Mary Wollstonecraft biopic “If Love Should Die,” starring Renate Reinsve and now shooting in Sweden. title: Vir Das Unveils ‘I Say We Run!’ Comedy Tour With London Residency, North American Dates (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 22, 2026 6:30am PT Vir Das Unveils ‘I Say We Run!’ Comedy Tour With London Residency, North American Dates (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Resident Evil’ Reboots at No. 1 as ‘Shaun the Sheep’ Bounds to No. 3 at U.K., Ireland Box Office 1 hour ago Parvathy Thiruvothu on Playing a Police Officer in ‘Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar’ and Speaking Out About Misogyny Despite Scrutiny: ‘I Enjoy Watching Patriarchy Fall Apart’ 6 hours ago Japan Pitch Heads to Busan Film Festival With Four Co-Production Projects (EXCLUSIVE) 7 hours ago See All International Emmy-winning Indian comedian Vir Das has unveiled his “I Say We Run!” comedy tour, opening with a run of 17 shows at London’s Soho Theatre in December before moving to North America in January. The London dates run from Dec. 7 through Dec. 23, including two-show nights on Dec. 12 and Dec. 19. The tour then crosses to North America on Jan. 15 in Ottawa, followed by stops in Toronto, Hartford, Philadelphia and New York before continuing through Ann Arbor, Minneapolis, San Antonio, Houston, Los Angeles, Monterey, San Jose and Santa Rosa. title: Mike Leigh Explains Why “It’s More Than Probable” That ‘Tender Loving Care’ Is His Final Film
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 22, 2026 6:29am Mike Leigh at TIFF 2026. Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for IMDb Beloved British auteur Mike Leigh has explained to the San Sebastian Film Festival why it’s “more than probable” his latest drama-comedy, Tender Loving Care , will be his last. The filmmaker appeared via video link at a press conference for the competition title, alongside producer Georgina Lowe and cast members Alice Bailey Johnson, Paul Jesson and Marion Bailey, who is the mother of Bailey Johnson and Leigh’s real-life partner. Their co-star Kate O’Flynn , who just won an Emmy for her scene-stealing performance in Widow’s Bay , was unable to travel to the film festival in northern Spain. Related Stories Business VFX House 22Dogs Launches New Facility at Pinewood Toronto Studios (Exclusive) Movies Red Sea Film Festival Cancels 2026 Edition, Vows to Return Next Year With "Renewed Vision" “It’s quite straightforward,” said Leigh when asked whether Tender Loving Care will indeed be his last film. “I have a medical condition [myositis], which affects my muscular movement, and it’s quite difficult to move around. [It’s] certainly more difficult than it should be for a filmmaker, and therefore it’s more than probable that this film will have to be my last film. That’s all,” he explained. “It’s a practical matter to do with my medical condition — a physical condition.” Leigh has touched on struggling with the condition — a disease affecting the immune system — a few times this year, as Tender Loving Care made its debut at Telluride, TIFF and now San Sebastian. If it is to be his last, The Hollywood Reporter called it “a lovely addition and likely conclusion to an exceptional career,” as Leigh, who was here in San Sebastian just two years ago with Hard Truths , once again shows his knack for gently gut-wrenching storytelling. In the film, O’Flynn plays a social worker, Amy, who moves in with her university pal (and fellow social worker), Rosie (Bailey Johnson). Amy is particularly close with her parents (Jesson and Bailey), who live nearby and are muddling through on lots of cups of tea. When a family health crisis strikes the characters later in the film, Leigh deftly tells us that much of British stoicism is actually courage, solidarity, and unspoken fear in the face of adversity. “Humanity is humanity,” said Leigh to the room of journalists about “reflecting positivity” and resilience amid “tough times.” He continued: “We haven’t stopped being human. The quality of life hasn’t gone away just because we’re in tough times — on the contrary, all the more reason to reflect positivity the way we can. Obviously, I hope that Tender Loving Care wouldn’t be misunderstood as a piece of romantic escapism because it isn’t. It’s a hard look at realities, but it is about compassion, and compassion is as important in these times as many other times.” With the film’s confrontation of post-War decline in Britain, as well as debilitating cuts to health and social care services, the director and his cast were asked about staying optimistic in the current climate, where, as Jesson eloquently put it, “people with lots of money […] run their countries brutally.” Leigh replied: “It’s a question with no black and white answer. One wants to be optimistic. One wants to see light at the end of the tunnel. I have children and grandchildren, and my youngest grandchild is actually two years of age. If everything goes as it should, he will be my age in the 22nd century, and I want that world to be a good world. I want his life to be positive,” he said. “On the other hand, it’s not difficult to be pessimistic because, as has already been referred to, so many things are happening in the world which are frightening and limiting. And really, that’s all I can say.” Bailey jumped in, explaining that she grew up in an age where she and her peers believed they were changing the world. She added: “I would say we have a moral obligation to try to be optimistic, but it’s very hard. But unless we are optimistic, we fail. And I’ll just point out, Alice is actually my daughter in real life,” she said, smiling. “So, of course I am concerned. I’d be concerned in any case about the future. I’m of the same generation as [her character] Birdie, and certainly when we were in our 20s, we thought we were going to change everything. We thought it was going to get better — that we were breaking down all sorts of horrible taboos and repressions that were around after the war, and that working people would have a better life. I would have been astonished to have known then what I see happening now.” In a lighter moment, Leigh was asked about the abundance of wine drank in the film — O’Flynn and Bailey Johnson’s characters have a few bottle-induced dance parties — to which he responded: “Drinking is part of our culture — certainly in the West or indeed in many cultures. As far as I’m concerned, it’s about making films about how we live at all kinds of levels in real life. Part of that is that people drink, so there’s a sort of symbolism in it. […] It’s not a comment about the pros or cons of drinking. It’s just the fact that it is part of the texture and fiber of everyday life.” Jesson added: “There is also a lot of tea [in the film]. I don’t think you should run away with the idea that most Brits are drunkards.” The 2026 San Sebastian International Film Festival runs Sep. 18-26. THR

title: California Vowed to Stop Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger. Why Did It Fold?
full_text: Skip to main content By Winston Cho Plus Icon Winston Cho View All September 22, 2026 6:16am California attorney general Rob Bonta. Getty Images Logo text For months, California attorney general Rob Bonta told anyone who would listen that Paramount ‘s $111 billion bid for Warner Bros. Discovery would ruin Hollywood and that he could stop the merger. Then, when his leverage appeared the highest, the political and economic realities surrounding the showdown became impossible for him ignore. That pressure came from the top. Gov. Gavin Newsom had expressed concerns about the state’s lawsuit, particularly in relation to employment levels. He had inserted himself into negotiations to encourage a settlement. “I’m very mindful of what this means to the state — our reputation,” he said at a press appearance last month, adding that he took CEO David Ellison’s threat to move out of California “seriously.” Indeed, Newsom’s fingerprints were all over the announcement of the settlement. Paramount thanked him “for his support throughout this process.” Read between the lines and the picture comes into focus: Newsom wanted a deal, and Bonta fell in line. Newsom leaning on Bonta — along with Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and gubernatorial nominee Xavier Becerra — put the state’s top prosecutor in an increasingly untenable position. California had sued to stop the merger, but it also faced the prospect of losing Paramount regardless of the outcome of the lawsuit if a deal wasn’t struck ahead of an Oct. 1 deadline when the so-called $7 million-per-day ticking fee starts accruing. That dynamic offers insight into how a case that once threatened to derail the biggest Hollywood marriage in decades ended with a whimper that stood in stark contrast to the political furor that spun off from it. This was always the likeliest outcome for the states challenging the deal. The government had signed off on the acquisition, and merger cases are tough to win in court. The states, especially California, were being asked to gamble on a trial whose outcome was far from certain. Still, that didn’t make the terms any less striking. While the settlement is broad in scope, it doesn’t require any divestitures that are typical of enforcer-friendly deals. Instead, it appears to be a five-year operating agreement imposed through a consent decree. Under the agreement, Paramount and Warner Bros. must release at least 30 theatrical films a year for the first two years and 32 for the following three, maintain minimum numbers of wide and independent releases and ensure that at least half of the films are produced or jointly produced by the combined company. They must keep 45-day theatrical windows and a 90-day SVOD holdback for qualifying films. A $30 million per film penalty is assessed for missing the annual quota, with divestiture of Paramount’s stake in Miramax in play if the shortfall remains unaddressed. The company also has to spend an additional $300 million annually on U.S. production (or $1.5 billion above its 2025 baseline over five years). Separately, the Paramount and Warner Bros. studio lots in Los Angeles must remain open and operate for the duration of the decree. Other notable terms: Keeping Paramount and Warner Bros. basic-cable negotiations separate and creation of a five-member independence board overseeing editorial standards at CBS News and CNN (selected by Paramount). A violation of the former term could see an order forcing the studio to divest from BET, VH1 and Comedy Central, among other channels (blue-chip assets like CNN or New Line Cinema are not on the table in these divestiture scenarios). If you said the settlement doesn’t go far enough, Bonta would probably agree. “I don’t think these two companies should merge,” he said at Monday’s press conference, titled “Attorney General Bonta Makes Announcement to Keep California Vibrant.” So why blink now? Here, the timing of the settlement is key. For California, the worst case scenario wasn’t only the merger being allowed to proceed but also Paramount moving its headquarters and hundreds of employees out of California while the case progressed. Call the threat a bluff if you want, but Ellison had been in talks with Tennessee and Texas officials leading up to the deal, with a decision expected at the start of next month. State politicians were clearly rattled as Los Angeles sees historically low filming levels. For Newsom, the departure of one of Hollywood’s most public-facing companies under his tenure as he teases a presidential run would’ve been a particularly unwelcome outcome. In the end, that risk outweighed a chance to stop the merger. The states certainly had a viable antitrust case, but it was a coin flip. They faced some of the best lawyers in the country too, including antitrust powerhouse Jeffrey Kessler, who most recently secured a landmark win for states suing Live Nation, Beth Wilkinson, who guided Microsoft’s bid to acquire Activision Blizzard across the finish line, and former U.S. Solicitor General Paul Clement, perhaps the most experienced Supreme Court litigator in the country. On the appeals front, it appears Paramount found sympathetic ears among the justices. The Supreme Court earlier this month told Bonta to respond to a challenge by Iowa and Montana looking to stop the antitrust lawsuit, signaling a potential review of the case that saw the government side with the studio at various points. Leading up to the settlement, it appears factions within alliance emerged on whether to accept the deal, with New York, Connecticut, Minnesota, Nevada as the holdouts. Ultimately, convincing California proved enough to overcome pushback from some of the other states, which faced the prospect of continuing to pursue the case without the state that would’ve been at the center of the trial. In a statement, Connecticut Attorney General William Tong expressed concern about the deal. The state “wanted and demanded full divestiture of CNN and CBS News. We wanted to save ethical and independent journalism and news,” he said. “We fought aggressively for that remedy. I am deeply disappointed that we could not do more.” Newsom also stressed at the press conference last month that Bonta is “not just representing the state of California, he’s also part of this coalition with a dozen other states.” The WGA’s statement illustrated the complexity navigating incentives and goals from each of the plaintiffs in the alliance while emphasizing the weight of the states’ decision to settle. “As a nonprofit, the WGA must contend with the reality of forging ahead alone, with no backing from government enforcers, with a complex antitrust lawsuit that would cost millions of dollars to pursue through trial,” it said. So now, Paramount is positioned to acquire Warner Bros. in a deal will create Hollywood’s next media and entertainment colossus. Faced with that reality, the rank-and-file are confronting an uncomfortable question: What good is all the talk about fighting consolidation if the political and economic costs become too high when the moment actually arrives to oppose one of the biggest mergers in industry history? title: ‘Heart of the Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt Is a Veteran Stranded With His Combat Dog in David Ayer’s Stirringly Crafted Survival-in-the-Wild Saga
full_text: Sep 22, 2026 6:01am PT ‘Heart of the Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt Is a Veteran Stranded With His Combat Dog in David Ayer’s Stirringly Crafted Survival-in-the-Wild Saga In spirit it's not far removed from an old Disney movie, but Pitt gives a true performance, and so does the canine actor playing his trusty companion. By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest ‘Heart of the Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt Is a Veteran Stranded With His Combat Dog in David Ayer’s Stirringly Crafted Survival-in-the-Wild Saga 41 minutes ago ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been’ Review: A Stirring Pop Doc Traces How the Great Singer of ‘He’s a Rebel’ and Other Classics Reclaimed Her Name 3 days ago ‘Resident Evil’ Review: Zach Cregger’s Reboot Is Funky Monster Fun, a One-Man-Against-the-Squish-Zombies Lark That Never Gets Bogged Down in Video-Game Sludge 6 days ago See All Scott Garfield In “ Heart of the Beast ,” Brad Pitt does something a lot of actors might not quite bring off in a man-and-his-dog-in-the-wilderness saga: He gives a true performance. His character, James Belmont, is a retired Special Forces officer who has been through a great many deployments. (There are combat flashbacks to what looks like Afghanistan, though the war isn’t named.) In the opening sequence, he’s piloting a small plane through the spectacular Alaska mountains, his trusty German Shepherd, Odin, by his side. Odin is battle-scarred, with titanium teeth and only three legs (he wears a prosthetic one). He’s a combat dog, raised by James since he was a puppy; having been through so much war together, the two have an animal closeness you can just about touch. Pitt shows you the love and trust James and the dog share, and also the veteran James is: alert, grizzled, taciturn, resourceful, a little too content to be by himself — but he’s that way because war has formed him, and how many others would understand? Related Stories Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago Billy Bush to Join Fox News as Contributor “Heart of the Beast” opens on a note of disquiet: Odin, standing alone in the middle of a road, as a young woman (Anna Lambe) approaches in a pick-up truck. So something happened along the way. The film then flashes back a week, to when the Alaska trip starts off as a bit of low-key R&R. For a while, we revel in the roughneck pleasure of it all. The grandeur of the skies and forests and lakes and snow-capped cliffs (the film was shot in New Zealand), the surreal quietude, the hiking through the woods, the serenity of pitching camp on a shore under the stars, the coziness of the campfire, the cooler of Belgian ale, the catching and eating of fresh salmon, the pouring of steaming coffee out of a tin pot — we could almost be watching a biopic about the Marlboro Man. All that’s missing is the lantern. Popular on Variety Pitt, in a beard and a buzzcut and camouflage shirt and aviator shades, with a compass tattoo under his left ear, is playing a man out of Hemingway by way of L.L. Bean. His James is so centered in this wilderness that he makes us feel at home too. It’s a telling feature of the movie that the character exhibits no overt war trauma; there’s almost a political layer to it, an undermining of the inevitability of the damaged vet. At the same time, you feel James’ war experience in the very premise of the film: his craving for isolation. Early on, he meets a stranger who looks like an old prospector (he’s played by J.K. Simmons), but after a few friendly minutes of light banter the stranger goes on his way. The only buddy in this movie is the dog. If it’s a surprise to see Brad Pitt holding down the center of a wilderness drama this tranquil and wholesome, the other surprise of “Heart of the Beast” is that it was directed by David Ayer, a specialist in reckless tales of urban violence and underworld nihilism (“The Beekeeper,” “The Tax Collector,” “End of Watch”). In a dramatic change of pace, Ayer and Pitt (both producers on the film) have teamed up to make something that isn’t so far removed, in form and spirit, from an old-school Disney movie. That said, the real surprise of “Heart of the Beast” is how well-made it is. Ayer draws on his logistical talent, and even his taste for violence, to craft a tale of survival that makes us feel the pain, the fear and the hardship, the stakes of what it takes to battle nature. We know something is going to go wrong, and without giving too much away, let me just say that James and Odin wind up stranded, without the plane, 58 miles from the nearest road. To survive, they’ll have to trek to that road, through the forest and the mountains and the plains — and since they start off by covering 8 to 10 miles a day, the journey seems eminently doable. They have supplies, and they can forage for food. But in this saga of man vs. nature, nature is not forgiving. The first obstacle is a grizzly bear, which approaches out of nowhere. The beast has been created with digital effects, which is the sort of thing that critics tend to pick at, but I’m interested in how scary and convincing the encounter is, and in this case the answer is: plenty. Ayer stages it with an awesomely meticulous danger. There are howling wolves. There’s a cliff that joins to the one across the white-water river below with a bridge made of two tree trunks. There’s a treacherous fall through the rapids. There is bone popping out of skin. Throughout, Brad Pitt projects a tensile strength, and a survivor’s moxie, that’s heroic but never superhuman. We see the physical anguish he refuses, and how the accumulation of wounds, even as he shakes them off, start to stack up. At one point, he thinks Odin is gone from this world, and when that turns out to be not the case, he weeps with gratitude. There’s a way to sum up “Heart of the Beast,” and that’s by saying, “This is a terrific performance — and Brad Pitt is extremely good too.” Because Uber, the dog who plays Odin, does one of the most affecting pieces of canine acting I’ve seen since the days of “Old Yeller” and “Lassie Come Home.” You feel Odin’s weariness, his intelligence, his dogged loyalty. The bond he shares with James emanates from the heart of both beasts, and that makes the film a journey stirring in its primacy. ‘Heart of the Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt Is a Veteran Stranded With His Combat Dog in David Ayer’s Stirringly Crafted Survival-in-the-Wild Saga Reviewed at AMC Empire, Sept. 17, 2026. MPA rating: PG-13. Running time: 101 MIN. Production: A Paramount Pictures release, in association with Domain Entertainment, Gulfstream Pictures, of a Wild Chickens, Temple Hill, Kino World production. Producers: Olivia Hamilton, Marty Bowen, David Ayer, Brad Pitt. Executive producers: Damien Chazelle, Scott Lumpkin, Cameron Alexander, Chris Long, Pete Chiappetta, Anthony Tittanegro, Andrew Lary, Sophie Cassidy, Zack Conroy. Crew: Director: Dave Ayer. Screenplay: Cameron Alexander. Camera: Mauro Fiore. Editor: Dody Dorn. Music: Jared Michael Fry. With: Brad Pitt, J.K. Simmons, Anna Lambe. title: ‘R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2’ Trailer Teases Cassandra Peterson’s New Role and the Curse’s Return (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Abbey White Plus Icon Abbey White Contributing Writer View All September 22, 2026 6:00am R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2. Tubi Something wicked this way comes in the new look at R.L. Stine ’s Pumpkinhead 2 . Ahead of its Tubi premiere on Oct. 9, The Hollywood Reporter can exclusively debut the sequel’s first full trailer. Helmed by Jem Garrard, the filmmaker behind the franchise’s 2025 installment, Pumpkinhead 2 once again follows kids Sam (Bean Reid) and Becka (Adeline Lo) as a new curse awakens in Redhaven. While still struggling with the fact that his family doesn’t remember him — a consequence of stopping the harvest curse — Sam and his friend Becka begin to notice strange things around town. To get to the bottom of this series of unsettling occurrences, the duo reteams and, in the process, discovers there’s a new crop of cursed pumpkin entities, conjured up by an ancient ritual book, just like the one that nearly took Sam’s brother Finn (Seth Isaac Johnson). Related Stories Beyond the Book Inside 'The Love Hypothesis': How Director Claire Scanlon, Star Lili Reinhart and More Adapted BookTok's Biggest Obsession Movies Nicole Wallace Joins Josh Heuston in Amazon MGM's 'Throttled' Adaptation This time, the friends are facing a series of child-like pumpkin-headed monsters, seemingly victims of the previous curse, called up from the ground of Redhaven. “I would like to go back to when one murderous scarecrow was the problem,” an exasperated Becka is seen telling Sam in the upcoming film’s two-minute trailer. Their investigative trail leads them to the town sheriff (Bob Frazer), who was responsible for keeping the first child-stealing curse alive. He reveals to the duo that he stole the cursed book from a woman named Cassandra, seemingly a local who lives on the edge of the town’s forest. Portrayed by Cassandra Peterson, best known by horror fans as Elvira, this wise witch has powers that may be key to helping the kids stop their Pumpkinhead uprising. “I can end the curse,” she tells Becka and Sam. “The magic is strongest on the harvest moon.” Working with others from the town, the duo once gears up to take on the powerful and deadly Pumpkinhead children to ensure no more kids are forgotten. “We don’t get to forget,” Sams says. Inspired by Stine’s The Haunting Hour , the Tubi film is written and directed by Garrard, and also stars Matty Finochio, Sebastian Billingsley-Rodriguez, and Kendra Anderson. Pumpkinhead 2 is executive produced by James Mattagne, Joan Waricha, Harvey Kahn, Yvonne Bernard, Dan Bernard, Jem Garrard, Allen Lewis, and Rama Diallo, and produced by Front Street Pictures. R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2 is part of the “Terror on Tubi” lineup. Timed to its release, Garrard and Stine will be joined by Tubi Chief Content Officer Adam Lewinson and drag queen and actor Jimbo ( RuPaul’s Drag Race UK and All Stars ). THR

title: VFX House 22Dogs Launches New Facility at Pinewood Toronto Studios (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 22, 2026 6:00am Pinewood Toronto Studios Courtesy of Pinewood Studios 22Dogs VFX, the visual effects studio behind work on Apple TV’s The Morning Show and the Netflix heist thriller Here Comes the Flood, has opened a new base in Toronto as its North American headquarters. The Milan-based international studio, with VFX credits also on Netflix’s Outer Banks, Lionsgate’s Day Drinker and Prime Video’s The Greatest, already has a Los Angeles commercial office in its global footprint. The new North American headquarters at Pinewood Toronto Studios will be the third production studio for 22Dogs VFX after facilities in Milan and Tenerife. 22Dogs VFX joins other global studios in Toronto doing visual effects magic for major studios and streamers chasing digital tax breaks, currency savings and lower labor costs in Ontario. The Pinewood Toronto Studios facility will be led day-to-day by Samara Melanson, head of studio, who will work closely with Andrea Marotti, 22Dogs partner and executive producer, based in the Los Angeles commercial office. “Since founding 22Dogs, our vision has always been to build a studio where creativity, innovation, and collaboration come together to support filmmakers at the highest level. Toronto is a natural next step in our global journey, and we’re excited to welcome new artists, partners, and clients as we continue to grow our international footprint,” Carlo Tosi, founder of 22Dogs VFX, said in a statement. The Los Angeles office will continue working closely with major studios and streamers and international producers, many of which bring film and TV series work to Canada for production and post-production. Pinewood Toronto Studios already serves as a Canadian production hub for Netflix and Amazon MGM Studios. “Toronto attracts leading creative companies from around the world, and we’re pleased to see 22Dogs VFX establish its Canadian home at Pinewood Toronto Studios. Their investment reflects the reputation of Ontario’s screen industry and further enhances the collaborative ecosystem our studios are known for,” Sarah Farrell, general manager of Pinewood Toronto Studios, said in her own statement. title: ‘Heart of the Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt and His Canine Co-Star Earn Your Tears in David Ayer’s Tense, Tender Survival Thriller
full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All September 22, 2026 6:00am Brad Pitt in 'Heart of the Beast.' Paramount Pictures If you’ve seen the trailer for Brad Pitt ’s new movie, you probably think that it’s a harrowing tale of survival in a dangerous wilderness. Don’t be fooled. Heart of the Beast is actually a love story, and one of the most moving to come along in a long time. That it’s a love story between a man and his dog doesn’t at all detract from its emotional impact. Indeed, Pitt displays an engagement with his co-star that may be his most resonant yet. Although to be fair, that isn’t really saying much since two of his most notable cinematic romances are Meet Joe Black , in which he played Death, and Mr. and Mrs. Smith , in which his character spent most of the film trying to kill his wife. Related Stories Movies Netflix's 'Cliff Booth' Trailer Has Brad Pitt Taking a Playful Poke at Leonardo DiCaprio Movies 'World War Z' Sequel Back on With Brad Pitt Returning, Edward Berger Directing Heart of the Beast The Bottom Line Packs a surprising emotional punch. Release date : Friday, September 25 Cast : Brad Pitt, J.K. Simmons, Anna Lambe Director : David Ayer Screenwriter : Cameron Alexander Rated PG-13, 1 hour 41 minutes The film, reuniting Pitt with his Fury director David Ayer , features the actor as James Belmont, retired after a 30-year stint with Special Forces that saw him facing combat in Iraq and Afghanistan. Now he lives a quiet, solitary life. Well, not entirely solitary, since he shares it with Odon, his beloved German Shepherd combat dog, with whom he experienced many dangerous missions. Odon bears the physical and emotional scars of his years in combat, sporting titanium teeth and an artificial leg, and suffering from PTSD-induced nightmares. The story begins with James flying his Cessna plane into the Alaskan wilderness (convincingly and gorgeously played by New Zealand) for a few days of camping and fly-fishing. The happy solitude is briefly interrupted by a stranger who happens by and spends the evening chatting away with the mostly silent James before taking off in a canoe early the next morning. He’s played by J.K. Simmons , making a strong impression in a brief amount of screen time and demonstrating yet again that he’s one of the most invaluable character actors in the business. An impending storm forces James and Odon to leave early, leading to the first of several surprises in the screenplay by Cameron Alexander. The plane winds up crashing into the water, not because of the weather conditions but rather James suffering a heart attack that renders him unconscious. Both he and Odon, who was thrown from the plane before it went down, miraculously survive, and when we later see James scarfing down aspirin by the handful we realize that he was well aware of his heart condition. Thus begins the survival part of the story, with James and Odon having to traverse 58 miles of wilderness to reach the nearest road. Along the way they encounter a variety of life-threatening situations, including a massive grizzly bear, a treacherous tree-bridge crossing over a gorge with rapids below, and an attack by a pack of CGI wolves. Both man and beast suffer an array of debilitating injuries along the way. But what makes the film special are not the survival elements, as grippingly and (mostly) convincingly filmed as they are, but rather the relationship between James and the loyal Odon, both of them constantly risking their lives for the other. Pitt makes his character’s feelings for his dog touchingly palpable, most notably in a quiet scene in which he removes Odon’s artificial leg and gently massages his stump. And while Odon doesn’t have much in the way of dialogue (he does have a very expressive bark), the way he looks at his co-star is so adoring and non-judgmental you may find yourself reevaluating the relationships in your life. Odon is mostly played by Uber (we can forgive the name), who would be the instant frontrunner for the PATSY Award if that worthy honor still existed. Credit must be given to his trainers, handlers, and Pitt himself, who reveals so much chemistry with his canine fellow actor that his previous female co-stars might be jealous. For certain scenes Uber is doubled by three other dogs, all of them his sons, which must have made for an especially harmonious set. Heart of the Beast sometimes feel repetitive in its pile-up of perilous moments, but Ayer’s expert direction and the fast-paced 101-minute running time prevent monotony from sinking in. And if the film’s ending leaves you dry-eyed, you’re clearly not an animal lover and someone I have no desire to meet. title: Neon Sets ‘Paper Tiger’ Awards Categories, Plans First Real Push for a James Gray Film (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Feinberg Plus Icon Scott Feinberg Executive Editor of Awards ScottFeinberg Follow Sign Up View All September 22, 2026 6:00am Adam Driver in 'Paper Tiger' Cannes Film Festival Paper Tiger , James Gray ’s crime-thriller starring Miles Teller , Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson , which premiered to strong notices at May’s Cannes Film Festival — including a rave from The Hollywood Reporter — and is set to open the New York Film Festival on Friday night, will be given a full-fledged awards push this fall by its U.S. and U.K. distributor Neon , The Hollywood Reporter can exclusively report. THR can confirm that as part of the campaign, Neon will promote Teller for best actor, Driver for best supporting actor and Johansson for best supporting actress, ending months of speculation about where the trio of A-listers would wind up. Related Stories Movies Inside NYFF's Splashy Lineup: Landing 'Artificial,' Weighing a Secret Screening and Opening on the "Miraculous" 'Paper Tiger' (Exclusive) Movies Korean Director Na Hong-jin on the Meaning Behind 'Hope' and His Sequel Plans: "Don't Be Surprised if He Crosses Over to the North" Paper Tiger , like many of Gray’s films, is semi-autobiographical. It tells the story of how a blue-collar family man (Driver) is enticed by his more ambitious brother (Driver) into an ill-advised business enterprise that ends up landing the two of them, as well as the man’s wife (Johansson) and children, in the crosshairs of the Russian mafia. Made on a $15 million budget cobbled together from a wide variety of sources (it has 24 executive producers listed in its credits), Paper Tiger is the sort of mid-range budget, adult-targeted American movie that almost never gets made anymore. Since its debut in Cannes, enthusiasm for it has been cultivated at the Locarno Film Festival, where Gray collected a special achievement award; and at numerous private screenings in Los Angeles, Manhattan and the Hamptons, which have attracted dozens of Academy members. Paper Tiger ‘s entire principal cast and all of its department heads will join Gray at its big Alice Tully Hall premiere on Friday night, and then on Saturday afternoon Gray will participate in a Walter Reade Theater conversation about the film moderated by a fellow chronicler of New York and one of his vocal admirers, Martin Scorsese. After that, the film will play at a host of fall film festivals — among them Mill Valley, Hamptons, London, Newport Beach, Chicago, Virginia and Savannah, with Gray set to collect directing honors at Mill Valley, Virginia and Savannah — en route to its U.S. theatrical release in select theaters on Nov. 13 and wider release on Nov. 20. Will it all be enough to finally land Gray — a longtime darling of critics and Cannes, but never a nominee of the Academy — and/or his film in the Oscar race? For a variety of a reasons, none of Gray’s prior films with awards potential received a fully-realized awards push. 2013’s The Immigrant , which was highlighted by a standout Marion Cotillard performance, was buried by Harvey Weinstein after Gray, who had final cut on the film, refused to acede to Weinstein’s demands for edits. 2016’s The Lost City of Z played on the closing night of the New York Film Festival, but then Amazon and Bleecker Street released it not that fall or the next, but rather the following spring, and it promptly disappeared. Gray did not have final cut on 2019’s Ad Astra , a big-budget studio film starring Brad Pitt, and it was taken away from him and re-edited by 20th Century Fox, resulting in a version that Gray has disavowed. (It did become the only Gray film to land an Oscar nom, best visual effects.) And Focus largely scrapped its campaign for 2022’s Armageddon Time after it underperformed commercially. Neon, which acquired the film last April, after it was completed but before Cannes, is said to be firmly committed to breaking that streak. A full breakdown of the awards categories for which Paper Tiger will be pushed appears below. BEST PICTURE James Gray, p.g.a. Anthony Katagas, p.g.a. Rodrigo Teixeira, p.g.a. full_text: Sep 22, 2026 6:00am PT Billy Bush to Join Fox News as Contributor By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest MS NOW, CNN, Politico Allege Trump, White House Staffers Violated First Amendment in New Suit 1 day ago ‘This Week’ Executive Producer Ready to Scramble for Midterms 5 days ago CookUnity Serves Gourmet Meals in New York City Bodegas With Spicy Promotional Recipe 5 days ago See All Getty Billy Bush , the longtime entertainment-news correspondent, is expected to join Fox News Media as a contributor, a potential sign that the outlet is growing more eager to cover the worlds of celebrity and popular culture with more depth. Bush’s new role is expected to be unveiled Tuesday, and he is slated to appear on Fox News Channel ‘s “Jesse Watters Primetime” in the 8 p.m. hour. He is expected to appear across multiple Fox News Media platforms. Related Stories Maria Bartiromo Out at Fox News, Fox Business Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago Bush has covered Hollywood for years, most famously as the East Coast correspondent for “Access Hollywood,” but also as a host for “Extra.” He had a short stint as a co-host of the third hour of NBC’s “Today.” In recent years, he has gone the independent route, hosting “Hot Mics with Billy Bush,” a digital program that looks as sports, politics, entertainment, technology and popular culture. He is expected to continue with his own ventures. Popular on Variety “I’m excited to join Fox News Media and its loyal audience to share my perspective on the people, ideas and moments shaping today’s culture…. as well as the ones trying to undo it!” Bush said in a statement Bush has grappled with notoriety and cancel culture. He found himself out of work for three years after a surreal incident in which a 2016 “Access” outtake was released showing then-Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump telling Bush about how he was able to sexually assault women. Information about the incident leaked from NBCUniversal and broke in The Washington Post , and Bush, who by then had moved over to NBC’s “Today,” lost his job . Bush has covered major live entertainment events, including the Golden Globes, Grammys and Academy Awards. He covered the Olympics from 2004 to 2016 on NBC and reported live from Prince William’s wedding to Catherine Middleton for NBC News. He has made several appearances in movies and TV shows. Bush is the nephew of the late President George H.W. Bush and the cousin of former President George W. Bush and former Florida Governor Jeb Bush. title: ‘Heart Of The Beast’ Review: Brad Pitt And A Soulful German Shepherd Struggle To Survive The Wilderness In An Emotional Journey That Will Have You Sobbing
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Forgotten Island’ Review: H.E.R. And Dave Franco Give Life To Gorgeously Animated And Frenetic ‘Toon ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Oscar-Predictive Toronto Film Festival People’s Choice Award ‘Magazine’ Review: Lily McInerny And Bright Young Cast Give Flavor To Pre-Digital Vanishing Era Of NY’s Literary World – Toronto Film Festival View All September 22, 2026 6:00am Brad Pitt and Odin in Heart Of The Beast Paramount Pictures Going to see Heart Of The Beast is a dangerous proposition if you don’t want to be seen crying uncontrollably in public. This man and his dog story is an emotional roller coaster that lays it all out there, and I lapped it up just like I did in My Dog Skip, Turner & Hooch, K9, Marley & Me, Old Yeller, and countless others. But there was something visceral about this one, a largely dialogue-less film where the story is told in the eyes of Brad Pitt playing opposite a loyal and tough German Shepherd named Odin. This is a story of a 30 year military veteran and the dog who stood with him in Iraq and Afghanistan only to finally find peace in the Alaskan wilderness until the unthinkable happens and it becomes an even greater tale of survival against all odds. It stays with you, won’t let go, and gives you new appreciation for those who serve, whether on two feet or four paws. Related Stories News Post-Merger Paramount May Overdeliver On Settlement Terms With 36-Film 2027 Slate Amid Speculation About Duplication & WB Leadership News Paramount Settlement Protects Pluto TV, Sets BET & Comedy Central As Potential Divesture Targets While Omitting Premium Channels & TV Studios David Ayer who directed Pitt in the terrific 2014 tank movie, Fury, here gets perhaps the most moving performance the actor has ever given. He plays Sgt. Major James Belmont whose military service is behind him and has come to the peace and solitary serenity of the wilderness, flying his plane, his dog, aka Canine Commander Odin by his side. It is as if this pair simply survived hell on earth to one day find heaven together. Watch on Deadline We see them all alone among nature’s wonders, until one day a stranger just appears out of nowhere. James hoists his gun but isn’t necessary. The man, Watkins (nicely played by J.K. Simmons ) is a friendly guy just looking for a little company before rowing off on his boat down the river. It turns out to be a welcome interlude, brief but meaningful. He will be the only human being James and Odin encounter together on their journey. Both suffer from bouts with PTSD, and James comforts Odin after disturbing nightmares shake him. It gets real when James suffers a heart attack and the plane careens out of control, finally landing in the water and sinking. Odin is thrown out before that, and somehow James survives and struggles to go back frantically trying to find his dog. He does even as Odin shows little signs of life, but after a night willing him to live, Odin, who wears a prosthetic leg and has few teeth due to another cruel war injury, clearly has a knack to survive and the next morning he is miraculously back to his old self. Using his expertise with a map and a compass, James and Odin set out to somehow find a semblance of civilization but the trip becomes one harrowing hazard after another including a frightening confrontation with a grizzly bear, a fight with a pack of wolves, James being swept away down the river, and more things most people could never live to tell. This is a pair that survived the worst of war (brief flashbacks briefly show that aspect of their past shared life) and now are unexpectedly in survival mode once again. His heart failing, James inherently knows his own days may be numbered, but he is going to make sure they find the road for reasons he doesn’t share with Odin, or Odie as he calls him. Heart Of The Beast is one of those movies that, with great dignity and little fanfare, shows the true connection between man and animal just as countless movies have done since Rin Tin Tin starred in silent pictures. That Ayer, with a heart wrenching screenplay by first time writer Cameron Alexander, has found a way to make it all feel fresh is why this director should be applauded. The success of the film is also due in no small part to Pitt who makes us believe this animal is his soul brother, much more than just a pet, or even a partner in combat. Odin is all he has left and he will honor him no matter what it takes. No spoiler but Pitt will simply break your heart in doing just that. As for Odin, has any dog ever won an Oscar? Lassie, Benji, anyone? Well, it is high time. Odin delivers one of the best performances by an actor this year, hands down. Actually the truth is he is played by four canines, the main star being Uber, with strong support from his own sons, Ryker, Zika , and Hondo. Give much credit to their trainer, Andrew Simpson. Other than Simmons and of course Pitt, the only other human on board is Anna Lambe as a woman driving her truck when in the distance she sees a dog sitting in the middle of the road. That is the opening image of the film, and then the story flashes back a week. I will leave it at that. New Zealand stands in for Alaska, quite convincingly, with stunning cinematography and camerawork from Mauro Fiore. As pretty as the natural landscape all is to watch it is still the gut wrenching emotional reach of this simple story of humanity at its finest, loyalty and friendship at its most meaningful, and above all the heart of a ‘beast’ and the man standing at his side. There will not be a dry eye in the house. If this one doesn’t move you, there is no hope. Producers are Pitt, Ayer, Olivia Hamilton and Marty Bowen. Damien Chazelle is among the Executive Producers. title: MIPCOM Bets On Creators, Brands & AI As International TV Business Readies For Cannes Get-Together
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart MIPCOM Bets On Creators, Brands & AI As International TV Business Readies For Cannes Get-Together Dhar Mann, Sean Atkins Set For MIPCOM’s First-Ever Pre-Opening Keynote Princess Diana Documentary Featuring Unheard Tapes Set For International Launch At MIPCOM View All September 22, 2026 5:06am MIPCOM in Cannes RX France MIPCOM boss Lucy Smith wants the world to know that October in Cannes is now about more than buying and selling TV programs. “Our biggest challenge is changing the perception,” she says, with this year’s event just weeks away. “You don’t come to MIPCOM just for your distribution deals anymore. You’re coming because you’ve got to find valuable IP, or you want to find out more about what’s going on in branded entertainment, or you’re looking at what’s happening in vertical drama or AI.” Distribution remains the spine of MIPCOM, but as the international TV industry has changed, so has its biggest annual get-together. “We are a marketplace, but it’s not just a buy-and-sell market anymore,” Smith says. Related Stories News Muse Entertainment Unveils 'Doula: A True Crime' Trailer As Boat Rocker Studios Boards CBC Doc News Dhar Mann, Sean Atkins Set For MIPCOM's First-Ever Pre-Opening Keynote That wider remit for MIPCOM means embracing the creator economy, brand partnerships and tech. Watch on Deadline Put simply, it had to change to stay relevant. Consolidation and industry shifts are impacting its core distribution business. For example, Warner Bros. and Paramount may have separate stands and spaces in Cannes this year, but that is unlikely to be the case when MIPCOM 2027 kicks off. The same is true of Banijay and All3Media. The medium-sized and small distributors, meanwhile, are feeling the pinch. Acquisition execs still attend MIPCOM in healthy numbers, but often with reduced buying power as their budgets come under pressure. Smith’s first MIPCOM was in 2006 and she now runs the market, which is organized by RX France. She says: “We evolve with the changes in the industry. We came out of probably ‘24 thinking, ‘This whole industry is just changing so much, and there’s less funding from traditional sources, so what does all that mean?’” The change under her leadership is visible. First, there was a heavy push into co-production and FAST channels, and then into brands and the creator economy. “We really wanted to make sure we were bringing more of the creative conversations around funding and IP. That was the first step, and then we brought the MIP Innovation Lab, so we could address streaming in a broader way. “And then, the big push had to be the creator economy.” YouTube had its biggest-ever presence at MIPCOM in 2025. It will be even more visible this time. Smith says partnering with the Google-owned company was “the right way to really make a mark and to say MIPCOM would be focusing and pivoting to the creator economy.” This year, Dhar Mann Studios kicks off MIPCOM, with a pre-market headline session on Sunday, before proceedings start in earnest on Monday. Powerhouse digital producer Mann and DMS CEO Sean Atkins will jointly keynote. “We all know that you know creator-led businesses are reshaping the global media landscape and we knew that that was that was something we needed to address,” Smith says. “We were getting calls from studios saying, ‘Hey, we want to meet all these creator-led businesses.’ And these businesses are really at that intersection of creators, brands and branded entertainment.” Having partnered with BrandStorytelling last year, RX France launches MIP BrandWorks this time to cover off its branded entertainment activity, with denstsu the headline partner. “We want to become the home of branded entertainment because we see ourselves as the gateway to the global entertainment content and media business. If you want to be working in content, and obviously brands need to be embedded in content to be culturally relevant, this is where you come and do that.” Artificial intelligence is also on the menu. A new conference and market will run under the MIP AI Entertainment Forum banner, with Versos AI and Protégé the partners. “Companies involved in AI and entertainment have a specific need to be part of the content industry conversations,” Smith says about the reason for launching the new forum. “You’ve got the studios and producers, the production side of things, you’ve got the workflow piece, and you’ve got the licensing part; those will be the pillars.” While the focus is shifting, MIPCOM’s USP remains bringing a critical mass of people together. In a world of Zoom meetings and with pressure on travel budgets, the numbers are not as big as in yesteryear, but no other international TV event gathers 10,000 people. “We know that bringing people together at one time in one place gives them the opportunity to work together on what these new businesses are,” Smith says. “We wanted to bridge the gap in the conversations between traditional media companies, who remain hugely important, and these newer creator-led studios.” Glitz and glamor are in the DNA of Cannes. The film festival and Cannes Lions lean into that with starry photocalls and A-lister parties. MIPCOM has the same setting and its own share of photo moments, but as it expands its focus, the event is still really all about dealmaking. “If you really want to do business and understand these new ways of doing business, this is where it’s going to be happening, and this is where things will start moving forward,” Smith says. ‘Gangs Of London’ Producers Suing Vice, Claiming They Are Owed $20M Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Diana’s Brother Over Memoir Which Midnight Madness TIFF Pic Could Become The Next Box Office Obsession? ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $108M WW Read More About: Comments

title: ‘Gangs of London’ Producers Claim They’re Owed $20 Million From Vice Over Pulse Films Sale
full_text: Sep 22, 2026 5:05am PT ‘Gangs of London’ Producers Claim They’re Owed $20 Million From Vice Over Pulse Films Sale By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Sees Mary Embark on Married Life in First Images 3 days ago Lego’s ‘Ninjago Legends: Duskfall’ Anime-Style Shorts Premiere in Korea Ahead of YouTube Release 3 days ago King Charles Denies Bombshell Book Claim That He Said World Would ‘Forget’ Princess Diana 5 days ago See All Courtesy of AMC/SKY The founders of “Gangs of London” producer Pulse Films claim they are owed more than $20 million over the sale of the studio to Vice Media in 2021. Thomas Benski and Marisa Clifford, who founded Pulse Films in 2005, allege Vice still owes them $20.43 million after acquiring their 22% stake in the company for $53.24 million. At the time of the acquisition, which brought Vice’s shareholding to 100%, the duo received $10 million in cash as well as a secured loan note for the remaining $43.24 million. Vice paid the initial installments but in September 2022 missed a payment of $5 million as well as subsequent payments, leaving a debt of just over $20 million. Popular on Variety Related Stories Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago Maria Bartiromo Out at Fox News, Fox Business Under the terms of the secured loan note, Benski and Clifford were entitled to force a sale of Pulse in order to reclaim the money. However, they claim Vice misled them into waiving their rights after fraudulently promising the parent company was solvent and about to be sold for a significant sum, which would enabled their debt to be repaid. The “true state of affairs,” they claim, was that Vice was “financially distressed” and “no genuine sale process capable of generating full repayment was underway.” Vice media filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy the following year. Benski and Clifford have not yet filed suit but earlier this month their motion for pre-action discovery, filed against Pulse Films, was denied by a judge in London’s High Court, who said the request for discovery before a lawsuit was even filed placed a “disproportionately heavy burden” on the company. Pulse Films said complying with the request would have cost more than £440,000 ($588,000) and involved reviewing over 264,000 documents. The judge said in his decision that while “it is not obvious to me that there is concrete evidence of dishonesty” this was effectively a question for a court to decide once a lawsuit has been filed. Variety has contacted reps for Benski, Clifford, Pulse Films and Vice.
