title: ‘Resident Evil’ Reboots at No. 1 as ‘Shaun the Sheep’ Bounds to No. 3 at U.K., Ireland Box Office
full_text: Sep 22, 2026 5:01am PT ‘Resident Evil’ Reboots at No. 1 as ‘Shaun the Sheep’ Bounds to No. 3 at U.K., Ireland Box Office By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Resident Evil’ Reboots at No. 1 as ‘Shaun the Sheep’ Bounds to No. 3 at U.K., Ireland Box Office 1 hour ago Juliet Stevenson, Olivia Williams Join Tim Crouch’s ‘An Oak Tree’ at the Other Palace (EXCLUSIVE) 5 hours ago Parvathy Thiruvothu on Playing a Police Officer in ‘Pradhama Drishtiya Kuttakkar’ and Speaking Out About Misogyny Despite Scrutiny: ‘I Enjoy Watching Patriarchy Fall Apart’ 5 hours ago See All ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Sony’s franchise reboot “ Resident Evil ” stormed to the summit of the U.K. and Ireland box office, debuting in first place with £4.2 million ($5.6 million) across its opening frame. Warner Bros.’ “ Practical Magic 2 ” moved to second place in its sophomore weekend, generating $2.03 million to bring its running total to $7.5 million. Studiocanal claimed third position with the debut of Aardman’s animated adventure “ Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom ,” which banked $2.2 million in its opening session. Related Stories Steve Doocy, Brian Kilmeade Will Commemorate 9/11 on Fox News After Covering it 25 Years Ago Maria Bartiromo Out at Fox News, Fox Business Studiocanal’s thriller “ Pressure ” took fourth spot in its second week with $1.4 million, pushing its cume to $5.8 million. Universal’s epic “The Odyssey,” directed by Christopher Nolan, followed in fifth place during its 10th frame, adding $794,765 to elevate its running total to $116.1 million. Popular on Variety Sony Pictures’ superhero blockbuster “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” placed sixth in its eighth week of release, collecting $772,975. The Marvel tentpole crossed another historic milestone to reach a running local total of $133.9 million, to occupy third position on the all-time U.K. and Ireland box office chart, sitting just behind “Skyfall.” Disney’s documentary “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger” took seventh place in its second frame with $659,899, lifting its cume to $5.1 million. Paramount’s “Bad Apples” bowed in eighth position with an opening weekend of $658,468. title: New Book on MGM Classic ‘The Women’ Reveals Extent of Joan Crawford and Norma Shearer’s Feud (Exclusive Excerpt)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Illeana Douglas Plus Icon Illeana Douglas View All September 22, 2026 5:00am 'The Women' LMPC via Getty Images Illeana Douglas ’ new book Jungle Red! The Making of MGM’s The Women , published on Sept. 15 by Lyons Press, delves into the titular 1939 classic which boasted an all-star cast of actresses — among them Joan Crawford , Norma Shearer , Rosalind Russell, Paulette Goddard and Joan Fontaine — and provided a template for modern female-driven projects like Sex and the City and The Real Housewives. In the following exclusive excerpt from the book, Douglas makes the case that the greatest Hollywood “feud” of all time did not involve Crawford and Bette Davis or sisters Olivia de Havilland and Fontaine, but rather Crawford and Shearer. Related Stories Movies Ann Blyth, the Evil Daughter in 'Mildred Pierce,' Dies at 98 Movies Casey LaLonde, Grandson of Joan Crawford, Dies at 54 Joan Crawford and Norma Shearer in a promotional portrait for The Women (Screen Archives/Getty Images) If MGM had been primed to sell The Women as “the Catfight of the Century,” they didn’t need to invent antics or drum up stories of feuds. Everyone knew that Norma Shearer and Joan Crawford really didn’t like each other. In March of 1939, before Crawford had even set foot on set, Howard Strickling had approved a Look cover promoting The Women that depicts Shearer and Crawford glaring at each other, with a headline that reads, “They Don’t Like Each Other… Inside Stories of 31 Hollywood Feuds.” On April 25, 1939, MGM’s production, listed as #1091: The Women , began shooting. A movie based on the stories of what happened behind the scenes might make a good sequel. When director George Cukor was asked whether he was fearful that longtime rivals Shearer and Crawford would try to upstage each other, he laughed, saying, “They’re too smart for those antics.” He was being optimistic. The best publicity angle, since there were no men in the cast and no juicy romances, was to exploit their longstanding “feud”. How much each actress fueled their “feud” is a matter of opinion, but since every squabble — the billing, the dresses, the trailers, and their eventual showdown because of Crawford’s knitting needles — was dutifully reported on, you have to imagine someone was spilling the tea. Anita Loos, screenwriter of The Women , said, “Norma and Joan could never have been personal friends— they came from different worlds. Norma thought Joan crude and pushy and Joan considered Norma overbearing and uppity — but they both knew the ‘feud’ was good copy, and so they helped it along.” When Shearer hosted a wrap party luncheon, chiefly to show the press how well they were getting along, Crawford skipped it. She seemed delighted to let the bad feelings percolate, telling gossip columnist Hedda Hopper, who was cast in the film, “So many people say Norma and I don’t like each other. Who are we to disagree with the majority opinion?” Shearer then refused to attend the premiere and penned an open letter to the trades downplaying her role and casting shade on the one actress she had least wanted to work opposite, Crawford. “I’m asked about the so-called power and influence I had at the studio. I don’t think anyone acted more like an employee than myself. Just because of my marriage to Mr. Thalberg, and as a consequence of my friendship with the other executives, there have been any number of times when I did not put up as stiff a fight as another actress would have. I didn’t want to appear to be taking advantage. For instance, I didn’t want to make The Women . I did make it, for the reason I just explained, and partly because I was taught by Mr. Thalberg to think of what is good for the picture as a whole rather than what is good for me as an individual.” Crawford had her reply teed up. She praised Russell for walking away with the film. Of her other co-star, Shearer, Crawford said, “Norma Shearer, as usual, played the perpetual virgin, the wronged wife.” She did give her one compliment. “I love playing bitches, and Norma helped me tremendously with this part.” When Cukor came on board to direct The Women in February of 1939, only one queen, Shearer, was attached, set to play the leading role of Mary Haines. She had seen the play on Broadway in 1936, and it was inevitable she would star in it. But when Shearer spoke to Hopper, who reported on every casting decision — including her own — Shearer distanced herself, saying, “You know, I hesitated a long time before playing this part. Then I decided that fighting to hold a husband is every woman’s problem.” Shearer referencing holding on to a husband when talking to Hopper was significant. After her husband Irving Thalberg’s death, she was in the process of reinventing herself. Doing a comedy about a bunch of bitter, funny wives complaining about men, when her husband was gone, was not in sync with her carefully crafted image of herself as the grieving widow of a man who was already gaining mythological status. She could also read the newspaper. The Women was no longer a Norma Shearer vehicle but, courtesy of Hunt Stromberg, “George Cukor’s The Women .” Every day, names were being mentioned: “Suzanne Kaaren gets a role in an MGM picture on the strength of a single test. George Cukor picks her for The Women ” ( Hollywood Diary ). Shearer waited on the sidelines, nervously wondering who her co-stars would be. The stable of talent at MGM was vast, and with 135 roles up for grabs, Cukor was auditioning all viable options except, it seems, Crawford. In March, the press was reporting that Crawford had been turned down for the role of Crystal, while it was announced that eighteen-year-old Lana Turner had been cast. Hairstylist Sydney Guilaroff wrote, “When Norma was cast as the jilted wife, Joan Crawford set her sights on Crystal. She relished the notion of going head-to-head with Queen Norma, now without the protection of her late prince.” Crawford was resentful that even in Thalberg’s absence, Shearer was still getting all the plum roles. Stromberg promised Crawford that Idiot’s Delight would be her next film, but then Mayer decided to give the part to Shearer. “‘No tits Shearer,’” Crawford complained, “could neither dance nor sing and had no experience playing fast women.” Crawford had been looking forward to working in Idiot’s Delight with Clark Gable, and perhaps rekindling their on-again/off-again romance. Instead, it was Shearer he held in his arms. “She had no chemistry with Gable, and that’s what the picture was all about.” Crawford was envious that Shearer had just received, with the studio’s backing, her fifth Oscar nomination — for Marie Antoinette . MGM consistently threw their voting bloc to Shearer, while Crawford had never even been nominated, despite standout performances in Paid (1930), Grand Hotel (1932) and Sadie McKee (1934). She was not about to let The Women slip through her fingers — even testing for the role, something unheard of for an actress of her stature. Eventually she won over Cukor, convinced Stromberg the picture needed her, and beat out teenager Turner by telling Mayer, “The woman who steals Norma Shearer’s husband can’t be a nobody.” Crawford may have, as she said, “resented the hell out of Shearer,” but playing Crystal only made sense if she appeared opposite Shearer. Without her, Crawford would be left playing a supporting part, a “heavy,” as Mayer called it, and for nothing. Shearer was pragmatic. She may have feared working with Crawford, but she knew The Women would garner more attention if Crawford was in the film, but only if Shearer could control the narrative, like later claiming it was her idea to cast Crawford. In the opening credits of The Women , Cukor had the cheeky idea of depicting each actress on-screen as some kind of animal. Crawford is a leopard. Shearer is a young deer. An innocent little deer does not do Shearer justice. A more accurate representation would be a lioness, for Shearer persevered in the jungles of Hollywood, marrying the boss, becoming “the first lady of MGM,” picking up six Academy Award nominations, even winning Best Actress for The Divorcee (1930). But Shearer was threatened by Crawford from the day she was hired as Shearer’s body double in Lady of the Night (1925). As for Crawford, Shearer’s marriage to Thalberg solidified the rivalry. Less than a year after Shearer’s wedding, Our Dancing Daughters (1928) was released, making Crawford a breakout star in the public’s eyes, but not at MGM, and not with Shearer, who called Crawford “an ambitious upstart” and referred to her as “common.” Crawford’s chief resentment was that Shearer got the best female roles at MGM only because of Thalberg. After Crawford was relegated to a succession of dancing films, like Hollywood Revue of 1929 , and Untamed (1929) — an unhinged, “jungle-themed” musical — Crawford confronted Thalberg. “Why do you save all your good roles for your darling Norma?” she asked. “Don’t you think I deserve some consideration?” Thalberg punished her for impertinence and put her in Montana Moon (1930), a low-grade musical Western. In 1938, after being labeled “box office poison,” Crawford needed a hit badly and lobbied hard for Idiot’s Delight . The part of a former showgirl masquerading as a Russian countess, opposite Gable, seemed tailor-made for Crawford. Stromberg told her that Shearer wanted to play the part. Of all the slights, this was perhaps the biggest grudge Crawford carried into The Women . “I cried buckets over Idiot’s Delight ,” she said. After The Ice Follies of 1939 . Crawford was at a low point professionally. She needed a hit. Her philosophy of going after the role of Crystal was simple. “It’s going to be a good picture. I need a good picture. If I can’t get one of my own, let me sneak into someone else’s.” She convinced Stromberg to talk Cukor into testing her. Though intrigued by the idea of an on-screen rivalry, Cukor was not a fan of Crawford’s acting, which he felt was mannered. After testing her for Crystal, though, Cukor consented and told her the part was hers. What changed? Crawford was not shy about her open and persistent dislike of Shearer. Once, years before, when she was asked what she thought of Shearer, she smiled and said, “Well . . . I’m an actress . . . and she’s married to the boss.” Cukor may have decided, possibly with the influence of Stromberg, that the competition with Shearer would make their scenes sizzle. Crawford was excited, telling the press after she won the part, “Even people who didn’t like me admitted I had intestinal fortitude, taking my career in both hands and gambling.” When Hopper asked Shearer what she thought about Crawford being cast, Shearer graciously said she was looking forward to it, and that The Women was “going to be a fascinating experience for her.” Butter wouldn’t melt in her mouth, as they say, but before shooting began, she made sure her contract stipulated that only she would have top billing, with her name above the title. It was a battle she would later lose, first to Crawford, then Russell. Shearer arrived early her first day to check the set and saw that there were three star trailers parked side by side. In accordance with being number one on the call sheet, Shearer had been assigned dressing room number one, nearest to the camera. It had been redecorated for her in coral, pink and cream. It was also air-conditioned. Inside there was an upholstered floral lounging sofa where she could rest and practice her lines, with fresh orchids on her dressing table. Shearer noticed that one of the trailers — dressing room three — was sticking out one foot further than the other two. When she inquired as to who was in dressing room three, she learned it was Crawford. Russell had been assigned number two. Shearer demanded Crawford’s trailer be moved back one foot in accordance with the others. Crawford’s arrival had been accompanied by glowing stories from reporter Harry Mines in his Raves and Raps column. “ The Women has been before the cameras at MGM,” he wrote, “but not until yesterday did Joan Crawford start work. Joan has a new and fancy portable dressing room, decorated in mauve. It was difficult to get a peek at the quarters, as baskets of flowers took up most of the space. Miss Crawford’s friends have deluged her with posies and telegrams on her first day in production.” Crawford stepped out of her limousine that first day of filming accompanied by her maid. Her uniformed chauffeur carried her record player and records, and one of her beloved dachshunds, Pupchen, acquired during her marriage to Franchot Tone. Crawford had a special clause in her contract allowing her to bring Pupchen to the studio when filming. An insurance policy protected the company in case the dog ever bit anyone or barked during a take. Cukor did not have to worry about a barking dog. It was Crawford’s vocalizing to opera that could be heard loud and clear during Shearer’s rehearsals. Though the set was not far from her dressing room, Crawford insisted she be driven to it via limousine. Shearer later followed suit, always making sure her limousine arrived after Crawford’s. Hairstylist Sydney Guilaroff recalled that Cukor’s greatest challenge was not directing on-screen but trying to keep the peace off-screen. He wrote that one solution was to always keep the actresses busy, separating them whenever possible. If one was rehearsing, then he could send another one to a fitting, or have them get a hair and makeup test. That way they were unlikely to be in the same space at the same time. “This worked well,” he said, “until Shearer and Crawford had their one face-to-face scene together.” To rattle Shearer, Crawford called in sick, and Cukor had to rearrange the schedule. Harry Mines, in the Los Angeles Daily News , ran a story that Crawford was under doctor’s orders not to work, and was ill from a combination of “intestinal flu and arsenic poisoning.” It’s hard to believe Crawford came across arsenic on the set, unless someone slipped it in her tea! (Hmm…) After two days, however, it was reported that she had made a remarkable recovery — or at least was well enough to continue. “On her sickest morning,” Mines wrote, “Joan had to do her most important scenes with Norma Shearer. Despite the tough break, Miss Crawford sallied through, doing such a good job that few realized how bad she was feeling.” The scene in question takes place after the fashion show in Crystal’s dressing room. Mary Haines (Shearer), Sylvia (Russell), Peggy (Fontaine) and Edith (Florence Nash) discover Crystal is trying on dresses and has asked the saleswoman (Frederika Brown) to charge the clothes to Mr. Stephen Haines’s account. Mary crosses the hall to confront Crystal and enters Crystal’s dressing room. Cukor began to rehearse. What happened next has been written about and reported from so many angles it’s like the film Rashomon (1950). Every bystander recalls what happened with slight variations, but all agree on one thing: Crawford, after years of perceived slights at the hands of Thalberg and Shearer, saw an opportunity to get even, and she did. Without Thalberg, there would be no repercussions. Crawford perhaps even sensed there was a bit of schadenfreude from Cukor, the cast, and the crew, knowing this moment would come, and wondering which cat would draw the most blood. THR

title: ‘Gangs Of London’ Producers Suing Vice, Claiming They Are Owed $20M From Sale Of Pulse Films
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Princess Diana’s Brother Over “Bulls***” Claim In Bombshell Memoir Tom Cruise Earns Applause With Six-Minute Monologue On Why Art Beats AI In Filmmaking: “There Is Nothing Like Human” BBC Removes Blackface Sketches From ‘That Mitchell And Webb Look’ View All September 22, 2026 3:38am 'Gangs of London' Sky/Vice Studios EXCLUSIVE : Thomas Benski and Marisa Clifford , founders of Gangs of London producer Pulse Films , are suing Vice Media , claiming they are owed more than $20 million. Vice took a majority stake in Pulse Films in 2016 before acquiring Benski and Clifford’s remaining 22% shareholding in December 2021 for $10M in cash and $43.24M in loan notes. Soon after, Vice ran into serious financial difficulty, with Benski and Clifford alleging that the company failed to pay loan notes totalling $20.4M, breaking the terms of their sale agreement. The producers — who exited Pulse in 2022 — claimed that they were persuaded not to exercise their contractual rights by former Vice executives, who they accuse of making fraudulent misrepresentations about the company’s financial health and failed sale to Antenna Group. Related Stories News Could 'Gangs Of London' Be About To Move To Miami Or Johannesburg? Vice Studios Boss Amy Powell Says She Is Mulling Franchise Expansion News Pulse Films Exits TV & Film Game After 20 Years As Vice Makes Layoffs In London Vice Group entered Chapter 11 bankruptcy in May 2023. Three months later, a consortium of former lenders — led by Fortress Investment Group, Soros Fund Management and Monroe Capital — acquired the company after a bankruptcy auction. Watch on Deadline Vice Media’s position is that Benski and Clifford’s allegations are baseless and lacking in evidence. The company intends to vigorously defend its position. Details of the dispute emerged for the first time in a UK High Court ruling earlier this month, during which Benski and Clifford failed in their efforts to get Vice to disclose thousands of documents relating to their grievance. Judge Peter MacDonald Eggers dismissed Benski and Clifford’s pre-action disclosure application, but did not reach any conclusions on the merits of their case. Deadline understands that the producers will continue to pursue action against Vice and are currently assessing their legal options. The duo, who now run Magna Studios, declined to comment. A Vice Media spokesperson said: “Vice Media is pleased to note that the London High Court has dismissed an application for pre-action disclosure by Thomas Benski and Marissa Clifford in relation to allegations concerning events prior to Vice Media’s Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023. “Those allegations are groundless. In dismissing the application, the court relied on the vague, inconsistent and unsatisfactory way in which the allegations have been advanced. We will continue robustly to defend any claim, to the extent it is pursued.” Benski and Clifford’s pre-action disclosure application named four defendants, including Pulse Films and Nancy Dubuc, the former CEO of Vice Media. Pulse Films’ intellectual property, including Sky series Gangs of London , now sits under Vice Studios. Summarizing Benski and Clifford’s claims, Judge Peter MacDonald Eggers wrote that they have “advanced serious allegations of fraudulent misrepresentation and unlawful means conspiracy against the respondents [at Vice]. In particular, the applicants’ case is that they were induced not to exercise valuable contractual enforcement rights by alleged repeated and false assurances by the respondents as to the valuation, solvency and an imminent sale of the Vice Group.” He continued: “Whether the allegations of fraud and conspiracy can be established will be an issue in any substantive proceedings which may be issued by the applicants in respect of their claim and will turn on the respondents’ knowledge about the Vice Group’s financial position and the failure of the sale process at the time they were allegedly giving assurances to the applicants.” The judgment added: “The respondents deny the allegations of fraud and conspiracy, which they state are couched in ‘unacceptably nebulous terms, based on unwarranted inferences, and without any sufficient evidential foundation.'” Vice’s position is that its executives were not obliged to keep Benski and Clifford abreast of the company’s financial position and that they dealt with duo with “honesty and integrity” at “all times.” ‘Gangs Of London’ Producers Suing Vice, Claiming They Are Owed $20M Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Diana’s Brother Over Memoir Which Midnight Madness TIFF Pic Could Become The Next Box Office Obsession? ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $108M WW Read More About: Comments

title: Brixton Community Cinema Creator Abiba Coulibaly On Why She Decided To End The Popular London Film Club
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Trailer: Brad Pitt Revisits The Character That Won Him An Oscar In David Fincher’s Latest Movistar Plus Announces 2027 Slate, Including JA Bayona & Fernando León Projects, At San Sebastián Naomi Watts Says She’d Like To Work With Paul Thomas Anderson & Praises The Advancements Older Women Have Made In Hollywood — San Sebastián View All September 22, 2026 1:02am Abiba Coulibaly Next month, the Brixton Community Cinema , the roving cinema project that has quickly become one of the UK’s most admired film communities under the stewardship of independent programmer Abiba Coulibaly , will close. Coulibaly announced the cinema’s farewell season in August on Instagram . “The closure of Brixton Community Cinema is not to give up and abandon either, just to recalibrate,” she wrote in the statement. Coulibaly launched the BCC in 2022 as a pay-what-you-can pop-up cinema club. She programmed a wide variety of titles, but the cinema’s central focus was international repertory and arthouse films. Past screenings featured titles like The First World Festival of Negro Arts by William Greaves, Abdellatif Kechiche’s La Faute à Voltaire , and Sarah Gomez’s One Way or Another . Related Stories News Muse Entertainment Unveils 'Doula: A True Crime' Trailer As Boat Rocker Studios Boards CBC Doc News 'Trump TV' Promo Uses Clips From 'The Simpsons,' 'Seinfeld,' 'Friends,' 'The Dark Knight' & Many More The eclectic programming made the BCC a must-visit film destination for cinephiles in London. In turn, the cinema’s audience grew and so did its reputation. BCC pop-up screenings moved from small non-arts spaces in Brixton to venues like London’s Cinema Museum. Criterion’s Ashley Clark described Coulibaly as “fantastic” during an interview with Deadline earlier this year . So why end things now? Watch on Deadline Speaking with Deadline ahead of her final screening on October 6, Coulibaly explains that the BCC project simply grew at a pace that was impossible for one person to maintain. “The project had grown more than I ever expected,” she explains. Below, Coulibaly speaks with us in depth about how she built Brixton Community Cinema, what she learned about audiences during the BCC’s successful run, and what she has planned next. Films set to screen as part of the BCC’s final season include Margarida Cardoso’s Kuxa Kanema: The Birth of Cinema (2003) and Sanaz Sohrabi’s essay film An Incomplete Calendar (2026). Legendary artist and filmmaker John Akomfrah will also sit for a discussion with Ish filmmaker Imran Perretta. Scroll down to see the full lineup. DEADLINE: Abiba, you’re closing the Brixton Community Cinema. Why? ABIBA COULIBALY: I always knew it wouldn’t last forever. I was actually adamant from the start that it wouldn’t, because I knew the limits of the “pay what you can” model. So I think it was always more of an experiment. But it all came to a head, I’d say, a year to 18 months ago, because the project had grown more than I ever expected. I then felt I needed to do things like register as a CIC, get a business bank account, and start paying for domains. As I tried to scale up, I realized I didn’t have the time or money to handle all the admin and bureaucracy. I actually ended up losing a lot of time and money in the process. It was too much for just one person. DEADLINE: The cinema did really grow. I did a piece with Ashley Clark at Criterion about his great book on Black cinema, and he name-checked you and the cinema. I was surprised he’d heard of it considering he isn’t based in the UK. Did no bigger institutions or funders come along to invest or support your work? COULIBALY: I read that interview and was really surprised and flattered to see my name mentioned. Ashley and I actually grew up on the same road, opposite each other, but he’s a decade or so older. But in terms of people coming along, honestly, no. Firstly, the question of who you work with has been difficult. It has very rarely been possible to align values and access to resources. I never envisaged having to deliberate so much about working with organizations. Sometimes it would be that they aren’t based in Brixton or Lambeth, or maybe I didn’t agree with their political stances. But in terms of one-off project fees, yeah, sure, I’ve been approached; it would be something like £500. But never any big, long-term support. Generally, money and business aren’t my strengths. For this final season, a friend volunteered to raise some money, and they managed to get £2500 from WeTransfer. That has been our only major partnership or collaboration. DEADLINE: I’ve been to your screenings, and they were always very well attended. What did you learn about what audiences want from cinemas in 2026? COULIBALY: I felt my audience was seeking cinema experiences that could address their real-world concerns. They weren’t really seeking an escapist moment, but rather the space to discuss and engage with relevant things happening around them. I started the project in late 2022. The genocide in Palestine began in late 2023, and I tried at times to speak to that through my programming alongside other things going on in various other countries. I always got the impression that those were the events audiences really wanted to attend. But I also had many difficulties with myself as a programmer. I began with a lot of enthusiasm about the power of cinema. Over the years, that has dampened in some ways. That is also why I want to take a step back. I also got the impression from audience members that they’ve had so many weird institutional failings from both cinemas and arts institutions. It’s really got to the point where there are very few large galleries, museums, or cinemas in London that don’t have some kind of problematic scandal or history. I think people are really searching for cultural spaces which don’t feel so compromising, when it feels impossible to boycott and divest from every single cultural institution in London. Abiba Coulibaly at the BCC’s open-air cinema during the 2023 London Festival of Architecture. DEADLINE: Talk to me about this final lineup. You’re focusing on a large geographical area; there are films from Madagascar, Pakistan, and Malaysia. COULIBALY: To end this run, I felt I needed to choose a theme or location. I’ve always tried to steer clear of regionally focused programming. I sometimes find it a lazy way of attracting audiences. I’m also slightly resistant to labels. I actually saw that BFI Future Film created a little zine for its Young Programmers’ Festival, and inside they said, “Go to Brixton Community Cinema if you want to see Black cinema.” They probably thought it was a really nice way to shout me out, and I’m sure they’re sweet people. But that’s so funny because I show films from all over the world. Ultimately, I believe I’m from the best city in the world. When I was growing up, there was so much mixing between all groups of people. With this final season, I was thinking very clearly about the question: How do you reflect a city back at itself? DEADLINE: You’ve actually done a lot of really important work here. Screening films that people otherwise would never see or even hear about. Have you ever thought about consolidating it all in a book or publication about the cinema? COULIBALY: From the very start of Brixton Community Cinema, I focused heavily on printed material. I used to do a lot of program notes and zines designed by some very talented friends behind the publishing studio Em—Dash, who do all of the graphics for the project. I produced those less over time because it was so labor-intensive. But I have this amazing archive of essays, texts, and interviews that I’ve always thought would make a really great anthology that could also speak to the political moment. For instance, the third or fourth screening I ever did was Jafar Panahi’s Offside , during the 2022 World Cup. When the screening came around, the protests in Iran had really taken off. So, I commissioned a Tehran-based film journalist to write about what it would mean to rewatch the film in this moment. There are so many interesting texts like that that are not only great films but also speak to the social and political context of making the Brixton Community Cinema. It’s really just a case of money. All of the material is there; all of the ideas are there. DEADLINE: You’re not going away completely. You programmed parts of the BFI’s Sarah Maldoror season. Where will people be able to find you? COULIBALY: I’m freelance, so who knows. I’m also a programmer for the Open City Documentary Festival. That’s my one regular programming gig. I will also continue to programme independently. title: Muse Entertainment Unveils ‘Doula: A True Crime’ Trailer As Boat Rocker Studios Boards CBC Doc
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Muse Entertainment Unveils ‘Doula: A True Crime’ Trailer As Boat Rocker Studios Boards CBC Doc ‘Stuff The British Stole’ Producer WildBear Entertainment Reshuffles Top Team To “Get Ahead” Of Industry Transformation BBC Drama ‘Ministry Of Time’ Adds Adeel Akhtar, Ciaran Hinds & Eight More To Cast View All September 21, 2026 9:01pm EXCLUSIVE: Here’s a trailer for Doula – A True Crime , a Canadian doc series from The Walrus and the Whistleblower filmmaker Nathalie Bibeau about a bizarre criminal case of a woman who faked pregnancies. The three-parter, which will premiere on Canadian pubcaster CBC on October 7, looks into the story of Kaitlyn Braun, who aged 24, reached out to more than 40 doulas with the same shocking story: that she had been sexually assaulted and was in her third trimester carrying a stillborn child. We can reveal Boat Rocker Studios has acquired the international distribution rights to the Muse Entertainment -produced show and will launch it at MIPCOM Cannes next month. Related Stories Trailers 'Coven Academy' Trailer Reveals A Forbidden Love Triangle & Explosive Powers In Supernatural Witch Series News A+E Global Media Backs Lifetime Korea Series 'Oh! My Guard' Starring K-Pop Performer Jung Yong-hwa & Hong Seung-hee The doc is notable for including the first interview with Braun, who was hit with 53 criminal charges after doulas, who had helped her and provided pro bono services such as hours of phone and video calls and round-the-clock in-person care, began to question her narrative. Watch on Deadline After piecing together the pattern that had formed over nine months between June 2022 and February 2023, many found others like themselves and started a grassroots campaign for to alert authorities through a viral TikTok counter-offensive. In the trailer, we hear from several doulas shaken by their experience. “I can’t tell you I was assaulted, that’s not really what happened and I can’t tell that I was scammed, that doesn’t encompass what she did to me. I have to tell you the whole story so you understand,” says one. “I have no felt fear like that in my entire life,” says another later in the trailer. The one-minute clip ends with a camera making its way up a porch, where it is met by Braun, who smiles as she opens the door and says, “Hello!” The film was made over several years, and attempts to go beyond the sensationalist reporting that followed the story at the time. Braun conversed with Bibeau several times over extensive interviews and phone calls, offering insight into her actions and motivations. “Everyone knew that Kaitlyn Braun had committed crimes. I wanted to understand why,” said Bibeau, writer, director and producer of Doula: A True Crime . “The deeper I went, the less the story yielded to easy conclusions. Kaitlyn’s deception played on empathy, and the harm it caused was real. “But the very thing that made the harm possible was also what I needed to understand her. I’m drawn to the places where human behaviour resists a clean moral frame. And this story lives in one of those places – where empathy doesn’t get in the way of truth, but brings us closer to it.” Jonas Prupas, Managing Director of Unscripted and executive producer at Montreal-based Muse, said the story “could easily be reduced to its more sensationalist elements,” but that Bibeau had made it “into something nuanced, surprising and deeply human.” Mellany Welsh, SVP and Global Head of Distribution & Brands at Boat Rocker Studios, added the doc offered international buyers “a story they won’t find anywhere else.” Muse – known for the likes of Sullivan’s Crossing , The Kennedys and Nose Deep – made the show for CBC and CBC Gem, with the series premiering on October 7 at 8am ET on CBC. Prupas and Courtney Dobbins are exec producers for Muse. For CBC, Sally Catto is General Manager, Entertainment, Jennifer Dettman is Executive Director of Unscripted Content, and Michelle McCree is Senior Director and Commissioning Editor of Documentary. Related Stories News CNN, MS NOW And Politico Journalists Denied White House Entry; Colleagues Condemn Trump’s Ban News CNN, MS NOW And Politico Sue Donald Trump Over His White House Ban Among the studios and networks whose IP is used in the promo are Warner Bros., Fox, Nickelodeon, Sony Pictures Television, Disney and NBCUniversal. It’s not a terribly unusual move for the president, who routinely posts AI videos that lift scenes from hit films like Top Gun . It is, however, somewhat unique in its breadth. And perhaps that is the point. Trump TV is a promotional effort launched after the president banned Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House . The administration billed it “The Essentials Station.” Another (grammatically-challenged) administration pitch for the service was, “Not every big moment has made it on your tv, now it can.” The service provides a live feed of official events, seemingly without the razzle dazzle of which the president is so fond. Not every big moment has made it on your tv, now it can. 📲 https://t.co/3KwWkBZ69m pic.twitter.com/g4v7n2J04s — The White House (@WhiteHouse) September 21, 2026 The advent of Trump TV comes after the president denied Politico, CNN and MS Now access to the White House over the weekend, prompting outcry from other media and a lawsuit from the trio . CNN had the White House pool assignment for Monday and was scheduled to be the primary network for coverage. The other TV networks declined to replace CNN in protest of the move, and as a result, there was no TV pool on a day when Trump is traveled to New York. The lack of network-level production is apparent. Video posted on the White House YouTube channel this weekend includes a long, very unTrumpy nine-minute recount of a ribbon cutting. title: Elliot Graham, Oscar-Nominated Film Editor on ‘Milk,’ Dies at 50
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes , Carly Thomas September 21, 2026 8:12pm Elliot Graham Joe Maher/Getty Images Elliot Graham, the film editor who received an Oscar nomination for Milk and cut films including Steve Jobs , Captain Marvel and No Time to Die , has died. He was 50. Graham died by suicide Saturday in Los Angeles, according to the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner. The biopic Milk (2008), directed by Gus Van Sant and written by Dustin Lance Black, starred Sean Penn as Harvey Milk, the first openly gay man to be elected to public office in California. The film was nominated for eight Oscars including best picture and won for best actor and original screenplay. Related Stories Movies Anjanette Comer, Actress in 'The Loved One' and 'The Appaloosa,' Dies at 86 TV James Sloyan, Actor in 'The Sting,' 'Xanadu' and 'Oh Madeline,' Dies at 85 On Facebook, Oscar-nominated Milk producer Dan Jinks wrote that his movie “wouldn’t have come together in the way it did without [Graham’s] amazing work.” Graham then reunited with Van Sant on the romantic drama Restless (2011), starring Mia Wasikowska. Graham also won a BAFTA award (shared with Tom Cross) for editing the James Bond film No Time to Die (2021), directed by Cary Joji Fukunaga in what would be the film editor’s final credit. And he produced and served as film editor on the 2018 FX series Trust , about the 1973 kidnapping of teenager John Paul Getty III. Born on June 8, 1976, in Claremont, California, Graham got his first credit for editing the thriller The Last Minute (2001), directed by Stephen Norrington. Next, he handled additional editing chores on X2: X-Men United (2003), then worked again for director Bryan Singer as film editor on Superman Returns (2006). In addition to Danny Boyle’s Steve Jobs (2015), starring Michael Fassbender, and Anna Boden and Ryan Fleck’s Captain Marvel (2019), starring Brie Larson, Graham served as film editor on Bill Paxton’s The Greatest Game Ever Played (2005), Robert Luketic’s 21 (2008), Stephen Daldry’s Trash (2014) and Aaron Sorkin’s Molly’s Game (2017). He also did additional editing on films including The Amazing Spider-Man 2 (2014), I Am Michael (2015) and Beasts of No Nation (2015). THR

In addition, per Bonta, “For each film that they fail to make, should they fail to make any, $30M is paid to be split three different ways, but 90% of it goes to workers.” Watch on Deadline Despite all the pom pom waving that the house of Harry Potter and Batman are now one with the house of Transformers, Star Trek and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, the question becomes, how will Ellison’s Paramount wrangle this beast? We hear that as Ellison eyes his early corporate structure that one or two executives would oversee overall theatrical and film strategy and likely one or two executives would oversee each film brand. Note that this is all fluid and still in the works. In addition, how the new conglomerate plans to deal with the duplication of marketing and distribution groups is in wait and see mode. Per the release breakdown below, there are plenty of weekends where the studios are dating against each other on the same weekend. In most instances, it’s a matter of counterprogramming — e.g. May 21, 2027, when family animated Warners pic Bad Fairies opens against a new James Wan Paranormal Activity film. However, it’s arguably unprecedented for a major studio to shell out on marketing for two big films from two big labels in the same weekend. Note: It hasn’t been uncommon of late for a big studio to face-off against its adult specialty label — e.g. Universal going up against a Focus Features title. The one glaring tentpole-on-top-of-a-tentpole frame is June 30, 2028 where Paramount’s feature take of video game Call of Duty is up against DC’s Dynamic Duo. Also, there’s the situation of some serious summer stacking. July 2027 has James Gunn’s Man of Tomorrow followed by Crawl 2 (granted, it’s a counterprogrammer) followed by Ocean’s Prequel and A Quiet Place III. Timothée Chalamet as Paul Atreides and Zendaya as Chani Warner Bros. While the studios can operate separately, Bonta says when it comes to negotiating and creating a marketplace where there isn’t reduced competition, “We basically ensure the status quo competition with negotiations (remaining) separately. It’s as if the companies never merged. They can’t bundle their basic cable channel assets. We address that by making sure that the fees remain flat, for the three years between the merch company and the exhibitors, the theaters. And then the requirement, this incredible, massive requirement for production output, cures for the less part, instead of paying more for less. You have the flat fee requirement with massive increase in production. So that’s how we address the concerns about reduced competition,” explained California’s AG this morning. The multi-billion dollar question as far as box office goes is whether Warner Bros. Motion Picture Chairs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy make the jump to the new entity. title: David Ellison: Me, Move? I Love L.A.
full_text: × Skip to main content By Erik Hayden Plus Icon Erik Hayden Executive Editor, Business Erik_Hayden Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 3:17pm Paramount CEO David Ellison Valerie Macon / AFP via Getty Images Fresh off brushing past California attorney general Rob Bonta with a settlement in which arguably only minor concessions were made, David Ellison is ready to re-commit to the idea of keeping his Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery empire in Los Angeles. “Now that we reached and announced a settlement, we’re eager to get to work building a stronger Hollywood,” Ellison said in a statement. “Let me be clear: the newly merged company will be headquartered in Los Angeles. We aren’t going anywhere. Our history is here and this is where our future is being built.” This brings the mogul back in line with his tune circa February of this year, when he was making promises to California politicians about how he would boost local production and bring back glory to Hollywood’s hometown. Then California attorney general Rob Bonta and his posse of 12 states filed a lawsuit in July that seemingly had Paramount on the ropes. And then the whispers started. You know, Ellison and his family have deep ties to Tennessee , he could pull up stakes and move Paramount there. Texas officials want the state to be the corporate headquarters capital of the United States, plus they have lower taxes — how does Austin sound for a Paramount base? Even at the time, these hints were chalked up to a game of high-stakes chicken over the summer between Ellison and California. Bonta himself, in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter in August when he struck a more defiant tone about the lawsuit, characterized it as a “ Hail Mary ” move and said “it seems like they’re grasping at straws.” But with each passing day, and with the threat of a $7 million-per-day ticking fee that Paramount would have to pay starting in October, the threat of a relocation kept feeling a bit more serious. Also, other states appeared to start taking the rumors seriously, too, which probably helped kick up the dust even more. Now there’s a legal settlement in place between the 12 states and Team Ellison dictating some terms for what “Stay in L.A.” means. Per the consent decree, the Warner Bros. and Paramount lots in L.A. County can’t be sold during the commitment period, which is five years. (Right now the Warner Bros. lot sits on about 140 acres, including the Ranch, while Paramount’s Melrose Ave footprint is about 65 acres.) It’s worth noting that up until Ellison’s buy, Paramount had been headquartered in New York (Paramount has an office in Times Square), and only last year had moved to L.A. And outside of the studio lot infrastructure itself, there are no commitments in the consent decree for, say, having a new office complex in another market outside of L.A. WarnerMount (ParaBros?) is a sprawling empire, after all. For example, does a combined company that owns both CBS News and CNN need office space in L.A., New York and Atlanta? Paramount owns 14 properties totaling 2.1 million square feet of space while Warner Bros. owns 14 properties totaling around 9.5 million square feet globally, per a June report commissioned by L.A. County. There are plenty of real estate scenarios to walk through that have yet to be sorted. But the question was never really about the fine-print of where the corporate HQ was. It was about intent. Through this summer of leaks, the implied message from Team Paramount was that Ellison would be ready to potentially do damage to the Los Angeles entertainment economy if things didn’t go his way in the court battle. There were plenty of locales that would be happy to greet Paramount and set up a water tower and some soundstages. Just look at the production flight that had been plaguing L.A. for years on individual feature films and television series. Local officials feared that a Paramount move would be the straw that broke the camel’s back, despite California doubling its tax incentive annually to $750 million and pledges to cut red tape and make it easier to shoot in state. Now that things did go the way that Paramount hoped as far as the settlement, it may prove tougher to just hit rewind to when Ellison was writing letters in March to California lawmakers saying, “my expectation that the commitments I have made will preserve and expand good-paying film and television jobs in the area.” But as of this settlement Monday, we’ve now hit full circle in that regard. Next up, if the deal closes as expected in a couple weeks, is the plan to start finding those $6 billion in cost synergies between the companies while fulfilling the rules-of-the-road in the consent decree. If L.A. County’s own commissioned report in June is any indicator, there will be a lot of redundancies up ahead as the studios start integrating. “The merger places about 2,495 jobs in Greater Los Angeles County and about 6,000 globally at potential risk,” it estimates, “mainly in corporate, tech, real estate, and other shared functions due to duplicative roles across the two companies.” THR

The alliance is being unveiled today at a YouTube Festival in London. Creator Voices said its members will “leverage their collective reach” and “advocate for institutional recognition and deeper integration with traditional creative bodies.” Related Stories News Adam Conover Dates New Stand-Up Special 'Big Divorce Energy' News 'Bling Empire' Star Dorothy Wang Launching Wedding Series On YouTube The move comes after thousands of creators including Amelia Dimoldenberg put their names to a first-of-its-kind report from YouTube that found its creator ecosystem contributed more than £2B ($2.67B) to the UK economy in 2023. That figure rose to £2.8B last year, according to a newer Oxford Economics Impact Report, which said the number could support more than 60,000 equivalent jobs. When the report came out, its authors said they wanted the job of content creator to be given government recognition along with better industry representation and access to finance. title: ‘Forgotten Island’ Review: H.E.R. And Dave Franco Give Life To Gorgeously Animated And Frenetic ‘Toon
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Oscar-Predictive Toronto Film Festival People’s Choice Award ‘Magazine’ Review: Lily McInerny And Bright Young Cast Give Flavor To Pre-Digital Vanishing Era Of NY’s Literary World – Toronto Film Festival Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews View All September 21, 2026 4:05pm Forgotten Island DreamWorks / Universal Pictures You have to give points to DreamWorks’ latest animated feature, Forgotten Island , just simply for being an original from a studio system that rewards familiarity. And it comes from writer/directors Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado who proved with their own sequel, 2022’s Puss In Boots: The Last Wish that you could find clever ways to renew and energize existing IP, rather than just settling for what the audience expects. I suspect this one though will have the most appeal to a teenage female audience as it is centered on the BFF relationship of two young girls, besties since grade school in the Phillipines, who have lived a life of memories (they have matching charm bracelets to prove it) since being little kids inseparable from each other. Now on the cusp of seeing life taking them down separate paths, they are about to embark on their greatest adventure together ever. But will they even be able to remember it? That is the hook here as the opening of the film introduces us to the wild and wacky Jo, and the more serious-minded Raissa with dreams of being a scientist one day. Related Stories Casting Jenny Slate Joins Dylan O'Brien In Hulu Comedy Pilot 'Lex' News Jo Koy Sets Sixth Netflix Comedy Special 'Blue In The Face' At home in Manila they both dream of a mythical place that in their minds absolutely exists. During their lives they have been fed epic stories by the beloved elder Lola (Dolly DeLeon) which are vividly shared with her class by Jo. The film jumps ahead to the end of their high school years where Jo (the older version voiced by singer H.E.R. ) and Raissa ( Liza Soberano ) are at that inflection point. Raissa is accepted into Caltech in America and is going to be leaving, while meanwhile Jo is stuck in a menial job at a fast food joint. This will be their last night and they are going to make the most of it when they come upon a magical portal on the beach, the portal it turns out to, Nakali, that Forgotten Island. Watch on Deadline Next thing you know they have landed there, with absolutely no idea of just how they got to the place of their imaginations. They are about to find out in this play on memory and the importance of it in all of our lives. With colorful new appearances (Raissa now has wings and half a head of hair) they have gone down the kind of rabbit hole that infamous characters like Alice and Dorothy have tread in literature and movies before, but this place is something else. In quick and whirring succession they meet some real doozies starting with Weredog, Raww (voiced with style and fun by Dave Franco ), who claims he had just spent the previous 12 hours with both of them. He is a bit of a mess, embarrassed by his ever-changing appearance from human to dog and back again, mostly dog though. He will be their self-appointed guide thorugh Nakali, but he has competition from another new acquaintance, Bungi ( Manny Jacinto ) a cycloptic giant blue baby still stuck (literally) to his mother after all these years. We also meet the more restrained cave dwelling Batiba (terrifically voiced by Jenny Slate ) who is agoraphobic to her core, but lives with a collection of knick knacks it turns out have been stolen from other peoples memories, just not her own since she is deathly afraid of venturing out into the world. She promises to help Jo and Raissa get back to their own world in return for their own memories. Along the way we meet Daju ( Jo Koy ) leader of a tree brigade; King Truffle Wuffle (Ronny Chieng) lording over his own feifdom; and the impossibly vain and slick Prince Mermahn (Kevin McCann). As in every single cartoon aimed at kids there is also a villainess, and here it is The Dreaded Manananggal ( Lea Solonga ) who can magically divide herself down the middle and other horrific talents. She’s the wicked witch and evil queen of the piece but of course there is a reason she got to be so bad and we will find out in due time. Jo and Raissa must navigate all of this in order to get back to where they came from in this uber frenetically-paced journey. Crawford and Mercado (who clearly has added the Filipino flavor to this story) pack way too much visually, especially in the first half perhaps sensing today’s younger moviegoers have a bit of attention deficit. I thought this thing, beautifully animated with different styles creeping in and out and as colorful as it could possibly be, would never slow down to take a breath. But finally in the second half when the girls’ own hopes and dreams come front and center, and the emotional elements take charge, it does cool its jets just enough to take it all in. The main theme of saving our memories, and keeping them close comes through loud and clear and there is nice resoloution to all of this. The busy soundtrack has lots of catchy tunes, old and new, including an original or two from H.E.R. herself. Is this an animated movie I will keep in my memories? Not likely, but I think its younger (much) target audience will indeed be the ones who will find some cool things to remember and some sharp life lessons about the value of friendship. Producer of the DreamWorks Animation production is Mark Swift. title: Paramount-WBD Settlement Sets Up Editorial Independence Board For CNN And CBS News
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Donald Trump Vows To Appeal Ruling In Networks’ White House Ban Lawsuit, Even Though Judge Has Yet To Rule Paramount-WBD Settlement Sets Up Editorial Independence Board For CNN And CBS News Read The Proposed Consent Decree To Settle The Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger View All September 21, 2026 12:40pm Story Arc CNN; CBS News UPDATED: The potential ownership of CBS News and CNN under one corporate owner has generated months of fear, anxiety and loathing at both networks, but the Paramount – Warner Bros. Discovery settlement tries to resolve some of the issues with the establishment of an editorial independence board. Related Stories News WGA Gets No Writer Layoffs At CBS News, $17.5M For Health Fund As Guild Confirms Settlement Of Lawsuit Against Paramount-WBD Merger News Read The Proposed Consent Decree To Settle The Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger Per the terms of the consent decree reached with a dozen state attorneys general, the board will establish a set of guiding principles based on each network’s policies for “accuracy, independence, fairness and journalistic integrity.” The board will resolve any disputes between CBS News employees, CNN employees and management regarding any alleged violations of the principles. And it will monitor “adherence to ethical journalism as defined by journalism industry best practices and to editorial independence.” The decree also sets up who can serve on the body, made up of five retired or active journalists who have worked for a minimum of ten years, and who will be appointed by the combined Paramount-WB board. No more than two members may be affiliated with the same political party. Watch on Deadline “No member of any government or governmental entity, including federal, state, and local governments, may approve or have approval rights over members appointed to the Editorial Independence Board,” per the decree. Officers, directors or non-journalist employees of Paramount-WB also are restricted from serving on the board, whose members will have terms of three years. Paramount would have 180 days to establish the board. There is a designation of a monitoring trustee to oversee Paramount-WBD compliance with the entire consent decree, but that person will have “no role or authority” relating to news operations. A “force majeure” provision can be invoked for events including disasters, strikes, labor disruptions and economic recessions, among other things. A separate settlement with the Writers Guild of America includes a provision prohibiting writer layoffs at CBS News broadcast for five years, the guild said. What the AGs’ consent decree does not do is restrict a combination of CBS News and CNN. Nor does it give the board oversight over who runs the respective news entities, something that has been an issue as CEO David Ellison tapped Bari Weiss to lead CBS News after Skydance’s purchase of Paramount last year. That has raised concerns that the network would be steered rightward, or even in a direction more favorable to Donald Trump. Weiss previously worked as an opinion writer for The New York Times and founded The Free Press, the center-right opinion and analysis site that Paramount also purchased. As part of her changes, she ousted the executive producer of 60 Minutes , while some of the correspondents who were fired have alleged politically motivated interference. Weiss has defended her input to the show, saying it is part of the news process. As part of commitments to close its purchase of Paramount last year, Skydance said that it would install an ombudsman to take complaints over CBS News. The person they hired, Kenneth Weinstein, was not a journalist but the former head of the rightward Hudson Institute. Unlike the traditional role of an ombudsman at a news organization, none of the findings are made public. Other actions have triggered further suspicions, including that, like CBS News, changes would be afoot for CNN, including appointing Weiss to oversee that network as well. As he sought administration approval to purchase Warner Bros. Discovery this year, Ellison hosted a dinner for the Trump White House tied to the White House Correspondents’ Dinner, and he appeared at the president’s State of the Union address. Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the FCC, said that the “editorial independence protections included in this settlement remain untested, and there is good reason to be skeptical they will hold up once the ink is dry. Whether these commitments actually protect newsrooms inside CBS and CNN from political, financial, or regulatory pressure, or simply provide cover for further editorial interference, remains to be seen.” Seth Stern, chief of advocacy of the Freedom of the Press Foundation, called the consent decree’s oversight board “worthless.” He said in a statement, “It’s unclear how the attorneys general or courts can constitutionally hold Paramount accountable for the board’s actions or inaction without themselves interfering in content. The attorneys general might be fine with censorship when they’re the ones doing it, but what happens when successors with opposing political views inherit enforcement powers?” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the state AG lawsuit, told reporters that the independent board would “ensure independent, objective, fact-based reporting at CBS News and at CNN.” An independent board is unusual, not not unprecedented. A special committee was set up in 2007 to oversee editorial integrity at the Wall Street Journal , as Rupert Murdoch’s News Corp was looking to acquire the news outlet from the Bancroft family trust. The committee, though, does have a say in major newsroom positions, as it has to grant approval for the appointments of an editor-in-chief and editorial page editor. Comcast committed to an ombudsman when it acquired NBC Universal, with concerns over corporate interference in the editorial process. David McCormick, vice president of standards at NBC News, had already been serving as ombudsman in 1993, and expanded his duties to other NBCU news properties. ‘Gangs Of London’ Producers Suing Vice, Claiming They Are Owed $20M Piers Morgan Wins Apology From Diana’s Brother Over Memoir Which Midnight Madness TIFF Pic Could Become The Next Box Office Obsession? ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $108M WW More from this Story Arc Paramount WB September 21, 2026 Paramount Settlement Protects Pluto TV, Sets BET & Comedy Central As Potential Divesture Targets While Omitting Premium Channels & TV Studios September 21, 2026 Paramount To Keep Headquarters In Los Angeles Post-Merger: “We Aren’t Going Anywhere” View All Story Arc Read More About: Comments

title: Paramount Shares Fall After Antitrust Deal, But Business Minds Marvel At Favorable Terms

Santiago/Getty Images While Warner Bros. Discovery shares soared 11%, as is often the case of a company about to be acquired, while Paramount shares stumbled on news the companies’ merger will take another two weeks to complete. The stocks’ divergent movement came after news Monday morning of a settlement between Paramount and 12 state attorneys general. A parallel lawsuit filed by the Writers Guild of America was also settled. The agreements pave the way for the $111 billion deal to close, but Paramount CEO David Ellison told staffers in a memo that it would take about two weeks for that final step to occur. Related Stories News Paramount Settlement Terms Laid Out By CA AG Rob Bonta, Who Says Deal Is “Not A Blessing” Of WBD Merger News David Ellison Hopes To Close Paramount-WBD Deal “In Approximately Two Weeks” As He Hails Legal Settlement In Company Memo While Paramount’s beleaguered stock jumped 10% earlier in the day, it slumped in the last two hours of the day, possibly on the news that more time is required before the transaction can be completed. Paramount is on the hook for a “ticking fee” of about $7 million a day, payable to WBD shareholders, for every day past October 1 that the deal is not closed. Paramount stock settled at $9.91, its lowest closing price in a month. Watch on Deadline Fears of the ticking fee adding up to around $650 million per quarter ahead of a scheduled March 2027 trial date – a not-inconsequential amount for a company worth about $11 billion – shadowed the legal process in recent weeks. The state AGs and the WGA filed suit in July after federal regulators had approved the deal, and gained surprising traction in a series of early court rulings, giving opponents of the merger hope it would be curtailed or even fully blocked.

title: Paramount To Keep Headquarters In Los Angeles Post-Merger: “We Aren’t Going Anywhere&#8221…
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Paramount Settlement Protects Pluto TV, Sets BET & Comedy Central As Potential Divesture Targets While Omitting Premium Channels & TV Studios Paramount To Keep Headquarters In Los Angeles Post-Merger: “We Aren’t Going Anywhere” The Final Stretch: California AG Rob Bonta On How Settlement On Paramount-WBD Merger Came Together After Stalemate View All September 21, 2026 3:03pm Story Arc Getty Images Paramount is not leaving California — at least not anytime soon — and that includes both the company’s studio lot(s) and headquarters. The settlement of the anti-trust lawsuit filed by 12 state attorneys general calls for the Paramount, which is set to acquire WBD shortly, to keep both the Paramount lot on Melrose and the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank for the next five years. Related Stories News David Ellison Hopes To Close Paramount-WBD Deal “In Approximately Two Weeks” As He Hails Legal Settlement In Company Memo News Paramount Settlement Terms Laid Out By CA AG Rob Bonta, Who Says Deal Is “Not A Blessing” Of WBD Merger “We wanted those lots to be protected, they are part of the the broader solution, and I believe that the future of this merged company is in Los Angeles for many years to come for the foreseeable future,” California AG Rob Bonta said during his press conference about the settlement Monday morning. Bonta was asked about the status of the Paramount headquarters, currently located in Los Angeles. Watch on Deadline “I believe that will be the case, that they will have their headquarters in California for the foreseeable future,” he said, adding, “It’s not part of the deal, I believe there will be public statements.” There had been no public statements on the matter, and the fact that Paramount maintaining its headquarters in California was not part of the agreement raised a few eyebrows. Paramount Chairman and CEO David Ellison did not address it in his official reaction to the settlement or in his company memo Monday, the latter of which noted the combined company’s commitment to producing 30+ movies a year and expanding U.S. film production. Hours later, he stepped in to clear the confusion. “Let me be clear: the newly merged company will be headquartered in Los Angeles,” Ellison said in a new statement. “We aren’t going anywhere. Our history is here and this is where our future is being built.” This brings to an end weeks of tension that culminated in an alleged ultimatum that Paramount would move its headquarters to Tennessee, Texas or Georgia if the anti-trust lawsuit filed by the state AGs was not settled by October 1 when a costly ticking fee to WBD was set to kick in. Per the settlement’s consent decree , the bulked up post-merger Paramount “shall not sell or close the Paramount or Warner Bros. title: Paramount Settlement Protects Pluto TV, Sets BET & Comedy Central As Potential Divesture Targets While Omitting Premium Channels & TV Studios
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit: No Move From L.A., Terms Of Deal, David Ellison & WGA Reaction, Shares Down, Read The Document, More Read the full story By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Paramount Settlement Protects Pluto TV, Sets BET & Comedy Central As Potential Divesture Targets While Omitting Premium Channels & TV Studios Paramount To Keep Headquarters In Los Angeles Post-Merger: “We Aren’t Going Anywhere” The Final Stretch: California AG Rob Bonta On How Settlement On Paramount-WBD Merger Came Together After Stalemate View All September 21, 2026 5:27pm Story Arc Pluto TV Photo Illustration by Rafael Henrique/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Here is a concession no one really asked for — the settlement of state attorneys generals’ anti-trust lawsuit over the proposed Paramount -Warner Bros. Discovery merger includes a provision ensuring that Paramount will keep Pluto TV or another free, ad-supported streaming service for the next five years. Related Stories News Read The Proposed Consent Decree To Settle The Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger News Paramount Settlement Terms Laid Out By CA AG Rob Bonta, Who Says Deal Is “Not A Blessing” Of WBD Merger While Pluto TV is protected, the settlement spells out which cable brands Paramount will have to divest if it fails to keep carriage negotiations for the Paramount and Warner Bros. basic cable networks at arm’s length. The list includes two Par nets that already had been put on the block twice, BET (and its various sub-channels) and VH1 , as well as Comedy Central , with the company’s flagships MTV and Nickelodeon out of danger. Overall, television feels a little like an afterthought in the settlement, illustrated by California AG Rob Bonta’s opening remarks at his Monday morning press conference. He spent more than six minutes laying out the agreed-upon terms for film production and had only two lines about TV, one about the establishment of “a news editorial independence board to support CBS News’ and CNN’s continued editorial independence” and one that “Paramount and Warner Brothers are required to continue negotiating their cable packages separately.” Watch on Deadline With state AGs’ action focused on protecting jobs, there is nothing in the agreement that would prevent Paramount from combining some of its post-merger TV studios — Warner Bros. Television, Paramount TV Studios and CBS Studios — which will result in layoffs. Or any guardrails limiting the number of positions that will inevitably be cut when Paramount merges Paramount+ with HBO Max as the company had said. Movies and basic cable were the focus of AGs’ legal battle because those were the areas where there were strong anti-trust concerns. (The combined HBO Max-Paramount+ will become a major SVOD player but will not have dominance in the space.) Still, the complete omission of the TV (or film) studios is surprising, as is the lack of mention of Paramount’s pay cable network Showtime , which, like the basic cable nets, negotiates carriage agreements. That would allow Paramount to bundle it together with WBD ‘s market leader HBO in dealings with operators. Emphasizing that, the settlement’s statement about separate affiliation negotiations for Paramount and WBD’s basic cable channels carries the following disclaimer: “For the avoidance of doubt, this paragraph does not apply to other Combined Entity offerings (e.g., premium cable channels, streaming services, or broadcast)” The omissions are especially glaring given the attention Pluto TV got despite it not being considered in real danger and it having no counterpart on the WBD side. The Curious Case Of Pluto TV Over the past year, Paramount’s leadership has been bullish about Pluto TV, vowing to invest in the AVOD platform and grow it, which they have done in the form of a slew of library content acquisitions and making Pluto part of the company’s backend tech stack convergence alongside Paramount+ – a complex, lengthy process which has largely been completed. Long before the Ellisons arrived on the scene, Pluto’s star had started fading as rivals Tubi and Roku became more popular. Pluto, although it had been a pioneer of FAST when it was founded in 2014, fell back in the market-share race. Its co-founder, Tom Ryan, and other core staffers exited the company. Even so, the new regime has expressed optimism about aiding the potential of Pluto, which had been largely neglected for the previous couple of years. “I am a big believer in the FAST space,” Paramount Chairman and CEO David Ellison said on the company’s Q4 2025 earnings call. Pluto TV was talked up to advertisers at the Paramount upfront presentation in May as a key piece of the company’s ad strategy, with upgrades ongoing and more underway. Most recently, Paramount noted that “Paramount+ and Pluto TV remain at the center of how audiences discover and engage with our programming as we build an entertainment platform for the future” in its Q2 2026 letter to investors, with the company’s executives saying on the earnings call that “we do expect that Pluto will return to growth in back half of the year.” With Paramount making a substantial investment in Pluto TV over the past year, there has been no talk of shutting it down. That has now been put on paper for the next five years in the anti-trust settlement. Basic Cable Haves & Have Nots According to the settlement with the 12 state AGs, “Paramount and Warner Brothers are required to continue negotiating their cable packages separately — a negotiate-separately condition, preserving the competition that exists between them today,” Bonta said Monday, adding, “It will mimic them being separate companies, even post-merger.” As to how that separation will be ensured, the statement is a little vague, noting that there will be a “monitor” and a “state committee” that would assess any complaints. If Paramount is caught in a “material violation,” following a six-month cure period where the company can “come into compliance,” they will have to sell one or more of the following linear networks: BET (Black Entertainment Television, including BET, BET Gospel, BET Her, BET Hip-Hop, BET Jams, and BET Soul), VH1, Comedy Central, Smithsonian, Destination America, and Science. After Skydance’s acquisition of Paramount, the company’s new leadership has shared their intention to revitalize legacy cable brands such as MTV, Nickelodeon, Comedy Central and BET. The inclusion of two of the four on the potential divesture list is somewhat surprising but Paramount still has kept crown jewels MTV and Nickelodeon out of reach. Additionally, the company already has Comedy Central’s biggest program, South Park, locked into a Paramount+ streaming deal for the foreseeable future and just folded BET+ into Paramount+. The rest of the channels on the list are small and, amid linear TV’s continuing decline, Paramount likely won’t mind divesting them anyway.
